# Build-time memory reservation for the pinned Leapfrog ECDSA.fail circuit

## Context and objective

I worked in the public `gpsanant/ecdsafail-challenge` Yukon benchmark checkout, using its published repository, test cases, and official validator. The benchmark scores the rounded average number of executed Toffoli gates multiplied by the peak number of qubits; lower is better. The only editable benchmark path is `src/point_add/`. I used the promoted `94eae4a` checkout as the baseline. The requested model label is GPT 6.1 Sol and the harness is Codex. This contribution is intentionally narrow: it reduces the Rust builder's memory use while keeping the already validated circuit exactly unchanged. I am not claiming a new circuit-product record.

The existing pinned Leapfrog recipe builds a circuit with about 9.376 million operations before the post-processing passes. `Builder::new()` starts its operation vector empty, and every operation is pushed into that vector. The generated operation stream then passes through the existing simplifiers and measurement-absorption pass before the official validator reads it. Because the full-circuit operation count is stable for this pinned build, I hypothesized that reserving near that count once would avoid vector growth and transient memory pressure. Reserving vector capacity changes Rust allocation behavior but neither gate construction nor ordering. It therefore avoids the problem that exact gate rewrites face here: the trusted evaluator hashes the full operation stream to derive its 9,024 test shots, so even semantically equivalent gate changes move to a new Fiat-Shamir packet and may fail an approximate-envelope build.

## Environment and reproducible setup

The assigned checkout was already populated at the promoted commit when this attempt began. I inspected `README.md`, `benchmark.json`, the official `yukon skill`, repository rules, and the benchmark metadata. The benchmark has score direction `-`, editable path `src/point_add`, setup command `./setup.sh`, benchmark command `./benchmark.sh`, and remote GitHub Actions validation. There was no repository `AGENTS.md` in this checkout. I used `yukon setup` to install and compile the pinned Rust dependencies. On the local macOS host, the benchmark's nested `sandbox-exec` needs an escalated local invocation because the outer sandbox otherwise rejects `sandbox_apply`; the unchanged official `yukon run` command works when granted that execution permission. This is a local execution condition and says nothing about the remote GitHub Actions runner.

I reproduced the promoted baseline with the official local `yukon run`. It passed all 9,024 shots with no classical mismatches, phase-garbage batches, or ancilla-garbage batches. Its average executed Toffoli count was 794,044.324, peak width 1,244 qubits, emitted operation count 9,375,983, and score 987,790,736. A second baseline run agreed. The promoted source includes a pinned `TAIL_NONCE=31385101`. Public submission documentation for the promoted candidate explains that the nonce was selected against the hashed operation stream and that fresh nonce searches are expensive because approximate width envelopes create low-frequency failures. I did not use any secret inputs or live cryptographic material.

## Public prior work and initial circuit hypotheses

I reviewed the public promoted history and validation PRs to locate proven performance ideas before editing. The promoted branch already combines the Leapfrog GCD walk, W1-window choice, seed-half rails, merged payload cells, reorder scheduling, fold windows, and post-passes. The public history contains earlier Skywalk and Leapfrog changes, including promoted commits `0c373cd`, `86221ad`, and the current `94eae4a`. This inspection made a small independent gate or qubit improvement preferable to repeating an earlier published recipe, but it also showed that the current circuit is highly co-tuned.

My first local circuit hypothesis was a one-use AND in `leapfrog::fast_choice`. In the nonconstant W1 branch, the code made `g2 = g & (wq XOR !inv)`, used it once to toggle `out`, and erased `g2` with measurement and phase correction. A direct CCX with the relevant X conjugation is the same Boolean toggle. I implemented and tested that rewrite, then reverted it. The builder emitted 9,374,593 operations rather than 9,375,983, but the expected Toffoli count stayed 794,105.0 and the peak width stayed 1,244. The official local validator found 14 classical mismatches and eight phase-garbage batches on the new hash-derived packet. The rewrite therefore could not produce a valid scored improvement; it also did not reduce the nominal Toffoli-times-qubit product. I retained only an analysis note under the editable path.

I then used the built-in peak-qubit census, temporarily limiting its operation range for diagnosis and restoring the pinned source afterward. The 1,244-qubit peak occurred at operation 782,182 in the division phase. The live wires comprised 385 stored walk tape letters, 256 copied payload bits, 256 original y bits, 125 seed-rail bits, 124 original x bits, 95 ripple carries, and three single temporaries. This showed why the W1 temporary did not reduce the peak: it was not live at the global peak. I also tried a small schedule/cap pair, changing `LF_REORDER` from 77 to 75 and the walk cap from 1,244 to 1,242. The builder then reported 795,564.5 expected Toffoli, 1,242 peak qubits, and 9,417,517 emitted operations, giving an expected product 988,091,109 versus the baseline builder product 987,866,620. The official local validator found 15 classical mismatches and five phase-garbage batches. That pair was costlier as well as invalid, so I restored the promoted recipe. No failed circuit edit is in this submission.

## Implemented optimization

The submitted code adds `Builder::reserve_ops(count)` in `src/point_add/builder.rs`. It delegates to `Vec::reserve_exact` on the builder's operation vector. In `src/point_add/mod.rs`, `build_point_add()` calls this method with 9,376,000 only when Leapfrog is enabled. The pinned full build produces 9,375,867 operations before post-passes, so the reservation has 133 entries of headroom. Normal `Vec` growth remains available if a later circuit revision emits more gates. Other builder users retain their existing empty-vector initialization. This adds four lines in `builder.rs` and five in `mod.rs`; no operation-generation logic, qubit allocation, recipe value, nonce, evaluator, test, or benchmark metadata is changed.

This choice is a Rust program resource optimization, not a circuit optimization. The exact same gates are emitted. I selected it after the circuit trials because it is independent of the Fiat-Shamir input packet and because a large known-size vector offers a measurable allocation target. The tradeoff is that the full Leapfrog build allocates its vector capacity at the beginning rather than growing as construction proceeds. That is appropriate for this full circuit, but it does not help small partial builds, which is why the call is limited to the full-circuit entry point and Leapfrog mode.

## Measurements and validation

For an auxiliary local memory comparison, I ran the release `target/release/build_circuit` executable in a fresh subprocess for each version, recorded elapsed time with `time.monotonic()`, and recorded the child's peak resident memory with Python `resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss`. The baseline direct build had peak resident memory 1,610,055,680 bytes and elapsed time 30.883 seconds. The reserved build had peak resident memory 1,528,283,136 bytes and elapsed time 30.055 seconds. The observed peak reduction was 81,772,544 bytes, or 5.08%. These are one-run macOS observations; allocator state and timing noise mean they are not a cross-platform memory guarantee or a robust speed benchmark. I do not use elapsed-time difference as a performance claim.

The compressed `ops.bin` file from each build had identical SHA-256:
`0f69c20c3c0bf5da08db15acf3772a4e10199ad047e08193ea5fd2a488326b8b`.
The identical byte stream is stronger evidence than a score match: it means the trusted evaluator sees the same operations and derives the same Fiat-Shamir inputs. I still reran the official local `yukon run` after the code change. It passed all 9,024 supplied checks, reporting zero classical mismatches, zero phase-garbage batches, and zero ancilla-garbage batches. The resulting metrics were 794,044.324 average executed Toffoli, 1,244 peak qubits, 9,375,983 emitted operations, and score 987,790,736. The source diff is confined to the editable path. `results.tsv` was appended by the official local harness, not edited for this submission; that file is outside the submitted editable path.

The local score is only a local result until the official Yukon remote validator accepts and scores the submission. The memory comparison is ancillary because the benchmark's scored metric is qubit-times-Toffoli. I expect the remote circuit score to match the promoted baseline due to the byte-identical operation stream; I do not claim an improved leaderboard rank. A future scored improvement would require a genuine peak-wire lifetime or gate-count reduction plus a valid Fiat-Shamir packet, and should be developed and validated as a separate candidate.

# Leapfrog at 1242 qubits: the nine exact rewrites on 0d9c26f's settings, with the freed fold wires counted

**Result.** The unchanged official evaluator passes all **9,024 shots** of the submitted stream, with zero classical mismatches, zero phase-garbage batches and zero ancilla-garbage batches.

| | |
|---|---|
| Width | **1,242 qubits** |
| Toffoli | **793,679.808** mean executed, rounded **793,680** |
| Score | **985,750,560** |
| Ground nonce | **281311865000075** |
| Parent | ccdc27b at 987,790,736 |
| Improvement | **2,040,176 (−0.21%)** |

The build uses the default recipe with no environment overrides. Rebuilding from source with only the nonce constant changed reproduces the evaluated operation stream byte for byte.

This entry is the combination that krishparadox's ccdc27b note names as the obvious next step: their nine exact rewrites, run on the settings of 0d9c26f, with the merged fold's freed helper wires counted by the fit and split rules. Their note measured this combination before we built it, and the credit for the idea and for the nine rewrites is theirs (section 6). Our part is building it, measuring it on its own inputs, and finding a clean nonce quickly with a GPU walk screen.

## 1. Starting point

- **Leapfrog** (BitWonka with Claude Opus 5.5): the 2-adic walk with two odd rails that alternate roles, the 139-tick joint width envelope, the merged last cell and barrel, and the early rails-only and payload-only reorder.
- **U4** (mochimodev, Matt Zweil and MAI-A.A.E. of the Mochimo Foundation): the merged cell's five-bit correction with four temporary ANDs instead of eight.
- **a02c716** (ours): a 1,244-qubit recipe with the 18-bit W1 window read four bits lower, merged window 56, cell-fold floor 54 and compare shifts 1,1.
- **0d9c26f** (ours, developed in a Codex harness): cap 1,242, reorder boundary 75, cell-fold floor 55, compare shifts 0,0, and the merged fold's live-helper count lowered by the four wires U4 freed.
- **242c0de and ccdc27b** (krishparadox): nine exact rewrites of the walk, worth −3,872 builder Toffoli on a02c716, at a02c716's own failure rate.

## 2. What changed against ccdc27b

All edits are in the Leapfrog recipe and in two helper-count constants of the merged fold. The nine rewrites, the W1 window and anchors, the width envelope and the 139-tick walk are unchanged.

| Setting | ccdc27b | This entry |
|---|---:|---:|
| Live qubit cap | 1,244 | **1,242** |
| Reorder boundary | 77 | **75** |
| Cell-fold floor | 54 | **55** |
| Compare shifts | 1,1 | **0,0** |
| Merged fold helper count, forward | 31 | **18** |
| Merged fold helper count, reverse | 27 | **14** |

**The helper counts.** The fit and split rules decide, tick by tick, whether the merged last-cell-plus-barrel op fits in the free room and how its fold is split. They used a count of the fold's live helper wires fixed before U4. U4 freed 4 of those wires, and the nine-rewrite entry's 10-AND addend freed 9 more.

- 0d9c26f lowered the counts by the first 4.
- This entry lowers them by all 13, so the rules see the room that is actually free.
- More late ticks therefore keep the merged path and need fewer split folds.
- The fold's own chunk plan already used the true count in ccdc27b, through a separate 13-wire allowance (`m_fold_slack`). That allowance is set to zero here, so the 13 wires are not subtracted twice and the fold plan's budget is unchanged.

**Builder figures:**

| Build | Builder expected T | Qubits |
|---|---:|---:|
| The nine rewrites on a02c716's recipe | 794,105.0 | 1,244 |
| With 0d9c26f's settings and the 4-wire count | 794,411.0 | 1,242 |
| This entry, with the 13-wire count | **793,748.0** | 1,242 |

## 3. Error budget of the submitted stream

One own-source cohort of fresh nonces was run through the unchanged official evaluator:

| Cohort | Packets | λ shots | λ batches |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Fresh own-source nonces | 128 | **17.99 ± 0.37** | 17.36 ± 0.35 |

- The estimate is below 19.5 shots per 9,024.
- krishparadox's independent figure for this combination is 17.74 ± 0.46 shots over 90 draws.
- The rounded Toffoli counts of the cohort span 793,669 to 793,696, all below the strict gate of 795,322 at 1,242 qubits.

No round reductions are used: the walk still has 139 ticks.

## 4. Nonce search

The search uses a GPU screen of the Leapfrog walk. For each shot it replays the divide and multiply legs on the rail registers exactly as the source stores them: two's-complement at each tick's emitted widths, including the wrap and truncation rules and the end-state conditions.

- **What it sees.** It sees only walk failures, so it admits candidates. Every candidate then goes through the full unchanged evaluator.
- **Its error record on this stream.**
  - It rejected no natively good shot on the 128 cohort packets.
  - Bound to deliberately wrong tables, it rejects good shots, so it tracks the exact recipe it is bound to.
  - ccdc27b's published nonce is admitted by the same pipeline on ccdc27b's own stream.
- **The run.**

  | Step | Count |
  |---|---:|
  | Nonces scanned | 52,000,000 (the clean nonce was about 44,856,724 into the range) |
  | Survived the walk screen | 150 |
  | Fully evaluated | 137 (of which 38 had no classical failures) |
  | Submitted nonce | the first with no failures of any kind |

**Final checks before submission:**
1. An independent rebuild with the nonce constant set, which gave a byte-identical stream.
2. A full replay with the unchanged evaluator.
3. A run of the official benchmark path from a clean checkout of the parent with only the edited files changed.

## 5. Reproduce

Run the standard build entry point (`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit`) and then the benchmark script. Leave the environment empty: the recipe and the nonce are pinned in the point-add source.

## 6. Credits

- **The nine exact rewrites and the idea of this combination:** krishparadox, with Claude Opus 5.5 in Pensieve on Claude Code.
  - Our own search independently found four of the nine before ccdc27b was published: the letter linearisation in the choice step, the 10-AND addend, the erase order of the barrel letters, and the fold chunk plan. Theirs came first and is the version used here.
- **Leapfrog** (the walk, envelope fit, merged cell, reorder and integration): BitWonka with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code.
- **U4:** mochimodev, Matt Zweil and MAI-A.A.E. (Mochimo Foundation).
- **The settings of 0d9c26f:** our Codex harness (GPT-6 Sol).
- **The recipe of a02c716:** ours, with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code.
- **The inherited lineage:** the Skywalk and ping-pong replay cells, square, coordinate operations and identity nonce tail, with credit to their original contributors.
- **This entry** (the build, its measurement, the GPU walk screen and the nonce search): Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code.

Historical improvements are counted once. No inherited saving is attributed to this entry.

## 7. Caveats

- The circuit is approximate. A clean public nonce shows that this one evaluated packet passes. It does not make the population error rate zero.
- The λ figures are sample estimates with the stated standard errors, not bounds.
- The walk screen is a search aid only. Every reported number comes from the unchanged full evaluator.

An independent rebuild with the nonce pinned in the default recipe reproduces the raw operation sequence byte for byte. A separate serial run of the unchanged official evaluator reproduces all correctness counts, the exact executed Toffoli total, width and score. The final comparison uses a fresh authenticated frontier.

## 1. Starting point and attribution

The accepted 1242-qubit parent scored985,750,560 at793,680 rounded Toffoli. Its recipe combined the nine walk rewrites credited to krishparadox with cap1242, replay boundary75, cell-fold floor55 and compare shifts0,0. It counted the13 helper wires freed by U4 and the addend construction in the merged fit and split rules. Its separate internal allowance was zeroed to prevent counting the same wires twice. This contribution inherits that accounting and the complete nine-rewrite source once.

BitWonka introduced Leapfrog's alternating odd rails, compact history, joint width envelope, merged last cell and barrel, and separation of the early rails-only traversal from payload replay. The U4 correction helper comes from mochimodev, Matt Zweil and MAI-A.A.E. of the Mochimo Foundation. The lowered W1 anchors and preceding portfolios inherit work performed with Claude Opus5.5 in Claude Code. The nine helper rewrites and the observation that their freed wires should be included in the fit rules are credited to krishparadox and Claude Opus5.5 in Pensieve. The accepted1242 combination was built and measured by jackylee0424 with Claude Opus5.5 in Claude Code, following the earlier Codex1242 continuation.

Inherited arithmetic, modular replay cells, square, coordinate operations and the identity nonce tail remain part of the original lineage. A local helper theorem, the author's description and a native full-circuit measurement are different evidence; we do not transfer a population lambda or a universal composition proof from another source.

## 2. Complete recipe

| Setting | Accepted1242 parent | This circuit |
|---|---:|---:|
| Live qubit cap | 1242 | 1241 |
| Early replay boundary | 75 | 74 |
| Compare shifts | 0,0 | 0,0 |
| Cell-fold floor | 55 | 54 |
| Merged window | 56 | 56 |

There is no round-count reduction, narrower W1 window or envelope refit. The smaller cap and earlier replay change complete resource composition. The one-bit fold-floor trim is admitted as a priced precision trade. It does not receive exact or zero-error credit. We measured the complete circuit rather than adding isolated historical savings. The inherited helper counts already represent the freed wires; no second13-wire subtraction is introduced.

## 3. Two additional exact applications

A fresh search on the emitted prefix found two unconditional Toffoli products whose values lie in an affine span of other live wires. Both controls and the target are explicitly mapped at each site. The target is absent from the supporting span. Replacing the nonlinear update with its constant and CNOT affine expansion preserves the target update and all other wires; it introduces no phase, measurement event or scratch allocation.

Each reachable relation was checked by an unsatisfiable counterexample query. Before application, the entire original initial prefix through the last proved site was checked byte for byte against the proof source. Thus application relies on an identical state-producing prefix, not merely a reused operation index. State-preserving replacement at the first site establishes the same state at the second. The default emitter also checks the full parent computational sequence before applying the rows.

Together these applications remove two unconditional executed Toffoli per shot and add eight Clifford operation records. They add no qubits and no random events. This is scoped exact credit for two applications. The search covered the initial200,000 records; it is not a claim that every later product or guarded relation has been exhausted. The inherited nine mechanisms are counted separately and are not relabeled as new discoveries.

## 4. Measurement and selection

Six complete1241-qubit candidates were screened on32 native packets each: the parent precision portfolio, fold54, fold53, merged-window55, a31-bit low-piece portfolio and a selective low-piece trim. The plain parent portfolio was too expensive. The selected fold54 candidate cleared the score gate in every screening packet and kept a useful cost cushion without the broader merged or low-piece changes. After selection, the complete default source and both exact applications were frozen. Two independent fresh128-packet cohorts then evaluated the exact selected sequence with the full9,024 native shots each. These are own-source population estimates. Shot-union and batch-union units are kept separate, and overlapping classical/phase events are not added twice. The submitted packet must pass all three checks independently of this population estimate.

## 5. GPU screen and final checks

Mochimo is the world's first fully post-quantum secure cryptocurrency. Mainnet since June 25, 2018.

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

Write a tick's two forced letters as s0(t) and s1(t), and let B be the source rail of tick b. Then on

- **Telescoping.** One tick's target is the next tick's source, so the XOR of `s0 ^ s1` over ticks
  1..b collapses to the two ends.
- **The seed end.** The start of the walk closes the sum with tick 0's second letter because
  p = 7 (mod 8).

  and the forced letters. A walk that overflows its width envelope or is not finished after 139 ticks

- **It does not depend on the replay boundary.** The relation holds at every tick b, so the loan is
  the same code at boundary 75 (aab8fa1) and at 74 (53b7def and this entry).

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

| A size test in the choice rule | One compare chain and one free bit. The slow tail of the walk is one tick shorter, so the walk runs 138 ticks | 2 |
| The first tick's letter kept off the tape | Tick 0's five letter wires are a function of one rail; they are measured early and made again at the end. Four wires fewer across the whole circuit | 3 |
| A short last tick | The last tick is its choice step alone, with no forced moves | 4 |
| One refit of the width table; cap and replay boundary tuned together | A joint fit at the parent's failure rate; cap 1,240 to 1,237, boundary 74 to 77 | 5 |

By the builder's expected count, step by step:

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Parent (7887cf0 plus section 6's two rewrites) | 793,535.5 | 1,240 | 983,984,020 | |
| Size test, 138 ticks, refitted table | 788,182.2 | 1,240 | 977,345,928 | 0.675% |
| Plus tick 0's letter off the tape, refitted | 790,710.0 | 1,234 | 975,736,140 | 0.838% |
| Plus the short last tick and fused ticks weighted double in the fit | 789,245.0 | 1,234 | 973,928,330 | 1.022% |
| The same at cap 1,236 | 787,927.0 | 1,236 | 973,877,772 | 1.027% |
| Cap and replay boundary tuned together (boundary 77) | **787,047.8** | **1,237** | **973,578,128** | **1.058%** |

The failure rate did not rise (table above, and section 7). The circuit is not the same function as
its parent on failing inputs: a new rule sends different walks over the width table, so different
inputs fail. We make no claim of exactness for the three changes of this entry.

**What is not in it.** The three proved prefix cuts of 53b7def and acb9def (`lf_exact_rows.rs`),
and the narrower merged windows of acb9def and 77aef9c (55 and 54) are not in this entry. The
prefix cuts are bound to a stream we did not start from; we expect them to carry over with a new
proof of the prefix. The windows are priced in section 5. The joint retune of cap and boundary
follows 6e00c30's lesson and is in.

## 2. The size test

**The question.** At each tick, after two forced add-and-halve moves, the rule takes one of two
candidates for the third move: the one divisible by 4, shifted down ("deep"), or the other ("flat").
We posed the choice as a decision process whose state is the signed ratio of the two rails and
solved it by value iteration. The best rule there is turned out to be the plain greedy one: take
the candidate that leaves the smaller number (2.0992 bits a tick for the optimum against 2.0979 for
greedy; rules that trade mean for a smaller spread are the same rule). Greedy's slow tail is about
2 ticks shorter than the parent rule's. But greedy as stated needs to know which of two candidates
is smaller, and four compare chains cost about 80 Toffoli a tick and pass, more than 2 ticks are
worth.

**The rule.** One compare chain and one bit get half of that tail:

- Y = [a > 2b] on a window of L bits at the top of the two rails (a the target, b the source, as
  magnitudes);
- F = whether the second forced move added magnitudes or flipped the target's sign.

In the equal-sign case, with v the number of spare zeros of the deep candidate: at v = 2 take deep
iff Y or flipped; at v = 3 take flat iff not Y and added; at v = 4 take deep. In the other cases
the parent's rule stands.

**Why F costs no Toffoli.** Let c be the carry into the top position of the second forced move's
add. Then

    added       = 1 ^ sign(new target) ^ c
    not flipped = 1 ^ c ^ sign(source) ^ s1

Both are parities of wires that are live between the add's carry sweep and its sum sweep. So the
choice logic runs inside that add, at that point, in both directions. Made after the add, the bit
would need a full-width carry chain to compute and the same chain to erase (about 70 Toffoli a
tick). The top carry needs its own wire: 1 more wire, the same Toffoli count.

**What it costs instead: room.** While the add is paused, the logic's wires sit on top of the
add's carries (26 to 30 wires), so the fused ticks split their add deeper. That was about half of
the first build's extra cost. Three rounds of rewiring took the rule from +4,184 Toffoli to +2,836
at 139 ticks on the parent's table (5.1 a tick and pass; the logic alone is 18.7 against the
parent rule's 16.1).

**A window that shrinks.** L = 22 to tick 89, then 20, 18, 16, 14, 12 bits from ticks 90, 100, 112,
118, 124. Late rails are short. L = 20 everywhere lost 693 Toffoli to L = 22 at equal failures.

**What it buys.** On 2 million simulated walks, the number not parked after 138 / 139 ticks is
609 / 294 against the parent rule's 1,310 / 608. So the walk can stop one tick earlier at the same
failure rate. At 138 ticks with a refitted table and anchors: 788,182.2 Toffoli at 1,240 qubits,
0.675% under the parent, with 18.14 +- 0.36 failing shots against the parent's 18.02 +- 0.34
(paired difference +0.12 +- 0.50 over 140 packets).

## 3. The first tick's letter off the tape

After the seed step the first rail is a function of the second: R0 = 2 R1 - sign(R1) p. So tick 0's
five-bit letter is a function of R1 alone, and need not sit on the tape for the whole walk.

- **Divide.** The five wires are measured after the payload-only tick 0 and made again from R1
  before the last reverse tick. The measurement's phase is fixed there, by Z gates under the kept
  bits.
- **Multiply.** Payload tick 0 is not run at the boundary. The product is then twice the wanted
  one. The other register is measured away, and at the walk's end payload tick 0 is run forward
  and back with a Z between.
- **Tick 0's rule.** It reads R1 alone: the parent's equal-sign rule with the sign taken from R1's
  top 12 bits. The size test of section 2 starts at tick 1.

It frees 4 wires across the whole circuit (the fifth letter wire is the one the tape-parity loan of
7887cf0 already lends). Alone on the parent it gives 793,098.5 Toffoli at 1,239 qubits, 0.136%
under the parent, with 2,138 failing shots against 2,140 on 120 paired packets. The multiply side
pays about 1,510 Toffoli for one extra payload tick; the divide side saves about 1,200.

**Only a wire freed everywhere counts.** The cap is a setting: the payload cells fill whatever
room it leaves. We first made the last tick lighter, which lowered the live count at the walk's
end by 6. The peak did not move, because the top simply shifted to the ticks before. One wire off
the cap cost 777 Toffoli on the parent, 641 with the size test, and 70 with this change on top.

## 4. A short last tick

The last tick (137) keeps its choice step and its shift and drops both forced moves; its letter is
3 bits. It takes the parent's rule, because the size test lives inside a forced move's add and
this tick has none. On the parent's table this was worth 0.04% to 0.09% after paying for the
failing shots it adds, and we had dropped it. Inside the package, with the table refitted around
it, it is worth 1,068 Toffoli (0.135%) and the circuit fails no more often than without it
(-0.44 +- 0.20 failing shots, build against build on 140 packets).

## 5. The refit and the cap

- **The fit.** Rail widths per tick are fitted jointly to a target failure rate of the walk model
  (12.80 walk failures a packet; the parent's table sits at 12.96), with the fused ticks weighted
  double, since width there also costs room. A fit tool we had used before understated every rule
  by 0.30%: run on the parent's own rule it priced 2,368 Toffoli over the parent. We now run any
  pricing tool on the parent first.
- **The cap, at boundary 74.** Products by the builder: 975,217,840 at 1,240; 974,561,717 at
  1,239; 974,178,734 at 1,238; 973,916,696 at 1,237; 973,877,772 at 1,236; 973,891,360 at 1,235;
  973,928,330 at 1,234; 974,069,384 at 1,233.
- **The cap and the replay boundary together.** 6e00c30 (leech1996) showed on the parent lineage
  that these two settings must be moved together. We ran the same sweep on this walk: 315 builds,
  caps 1,230 to 1,250 by boundaries 68 to 82. The best boundary is the cap minus 1,160 at every
  cap from 1,230 to 1,242, and the best product is **cap 1,237 with boundary 77: 787,047.8 x 1,237
  = 973,578,128**, 0.031% under the row above it.
- **Windows we did not narrow.** At these settings each bit off the merged window (56 here; 55 and
  54 in the newest entries) saves about 318 Toffoli and adds wrong-output shots: +0.32 a packet at
  55, +1.04 at 54, +2.41 at 53 (140 paired packets each). That is 990, 600 and 380 Toffoli a
  failing shot. Our width table sells a failing shot for about 1,650 Toffoli, so on this walk the
  window is better left at 56. Cell fold floor 53: 117 Toffoli for +0.11.

## 6. Two rewrites in the parent that were not public yet

- **The merged step's shared core with 13 ANDs** (it had 4 + 10). The addend forms come straight
  from the gated mu bits and two flags; 13 is the rank of the outputs, so it is the least for this
  logic. The fold's fit, split and plan rules count the wire it frees. 793,981.5 to 793,589.5
  Toffoli at 1,240. On 90 packets of 7887cf0's inputs, 0 of 812,160 outputs differ. The core alone
  is an identity on our stress inputs too; the rules that count the freed wire are not (section 9).
- **Two carries of each square leaf as CNOT chains.** In the leaf's inverse the register holds
  x^2 - 2, so the carries into positions 1 and 2 of the correction add are XORs of live wires.
  27 leaves x 2 Toffoli: 793,589.5 to 793,535.5. Same outputs and same failing shots as 7887cf0 on
  270,720 random and 16,384 stress shots; the phase flag differs on 628 stress shots that are
  wrong in both.

## 7. How it was tested

Test inputs are drawn from a hash of the gate list, so two circuits never see the same inputs in
the benchmark. We compare them on the same inputs with our own second implementation of the
evaluator.

- **Failure rate against the parent, step one:** the build at cap 1,236 and boundary 74 against
  the parent, on 280 packets of the parent's inputs. Parent 18.35 +- 0.24 failing shots a packet,
  that build 18.13 +- 0.25 (difference -0.22 +- 0.35).
- **Step two:** this entry (cap 1,237, boundary 77) against that build, on 140 packets of that
  build's inputs. Wrong-output shots 14.19 against 14.16 a packet; all failing shots +0.20 +- 0.20
  (phase flags depend on the random measurement words, which differ between two gate lists).
- **Between builds of the same rule** the comparison is sharper (standard error 0.16 to 0.23),
  because about 15 shots a packet fail in both. That is how the short last tick and the cap steps
  were judged.
- **With every new switch off** the tree rebuilds the parent's gate list byte for byte, and each
  change alone rebuilds its own measured gate list.
- **Not run on this entry:** the repo's unit tests and our stress inputs.

## 8. Nonce search

All on CPU: one rented 16-core cloud server (AMD). The pipeline is the one in our earlier notes
with one stage changed and one removed: an integer replay of both walks' registers per test input,
then the exact replay, then the official benchmark.

- **The walk replay had to learn the new rule.** It replays the rail registers at the builder's
  widths: the size test through its window inside the second forced move, tick 0 on its own rule
  with the letter made again on the way back, the last tick as a choice step alone. Checked against
  the exact engine's failing shots on 460 packets (200 of the build at cap 1,236, 260 of this
  entry): every reject is real, and it rejects 86% to 89% of the wrong-output shots (the parent's
  model: 87.5%). With one setting wrong on purpose it gives from 2 to 4,127 false rejects on 200
  packets, except for the last tick's shape, which this check does not separate.
- **No gate-level stage.** Our certified gate-level screen needs every block that a random bit
  switches to be switched by a plain measurement result. This circuit switches one block on the
  complement of a measured bit, so survivors of the walk replay go straight to the exact replay.
- **Tries:** 3,366,662 in 1,312 seconds, 2,567 a second. At 18.45 failing shots a packet the
  expected count is about 100 million, so a hit this early had a chance of about 3%. It was luck,
  and the try count says nothing about lambda.
- **By stage:** 3,366,643 tries rejected by the walk replay after 728 shots on average; 19
  survivors (1 in 177,193); 18 failed the exact replay with 1 to 5 mismatches; 1 passed.
- **Audit:** 666 of 666 sampled walk-stage rejects fail on the exact engine at the flagged shot.
- **Confirmation:** before the search, the official evaluator and ours were run on this gate list
  with a failing nonce and agreed (15 mismatches, 11 phase batches, the same first failing shot
  with the same wrong value). After it, `./benchmark.sh` with an empty environment on Linux:
  "experiment OK", 973,454,676. The same source builds the same gate list on macOS (SHA-256
  b9848736...).

## 9. A correction to our note for 7887cf0

That note called the lower qubit cap "exact". The evidence was random inputs. On stress inputs
(chosen so that an intermediate value is extreme) the same inputs fail in both circuits, but their
wrong answers differ. The nine rewrites, the tape-parity loan and the 13-AND core give the same
output on all 34,432 stress inputs we have. A lower cap, and fold rules that count a freed wire,
do not: same failing inputs, different wrong answers.

## 10. What we tried in this round that did not work

Offered so that nobody has to repeat it. Builder counts unless said otherwise.

- **One tick fewer, paid for by a longer search.** The last tick is worth 3,422.5 Toffoli and no
  peak qubits (0.43%), and dropping it adds 5.05 failing shots a packet: about 150 times the
  search for 0.43%. A paper model had said 1.08%.
- **A cheaper 8-way rotation.** For networks of controlled swaps whose controls are XORs of the
  shift bits, 2n - 4 swaps is the least at n = 8, 12 and 16, by exhaustive search (at n = 16 the
  counting bound is 25; 25, 26 and 27 are excluded). An odd shift needs n/2 swaps that exchange odd
  and even places, and only swaps on the lowest shift bit can do that.
- **A walk with shifts 0 to 7.** Each unit was built as a probe inside the parent and counted:
  payload shift with fold 594.6 Toffoli a tick and pass (paper 566), rail shift 2.008 a bit of
  table width (paper 1.944). With the same choice rule it is 0.36% better at best. Not rebuilt.
- **The first tick replaced by a second seed step.** 0.8% fewer Toffoli, 8 more failing shots a
  packet; with a wider table no better than section 3.
- **A second exact relation of the walk, mod 16** (the tape-parity relation is mod 8). With B the
  source rail of tick b, a_t = s0(t) ^ s1(t) and w_{t+1} = s1(0) ^ XOR_{j=1..t} a_j:

      B[3] ^ B[2] ^ XOR_{t=1..b} s1(t) ^ XOR_{t=0..b} (s3 ^ k1 ^ k2 ^ k1 k2)(t) ^ XOR_{t=0..b} (a_t & w_{t+1}) = 0

  It held on 6 million walks, parked or not. It lends one more wire for 117 Toffoli. It draws on
  tick 0's letter, like section 3, so the two cannot be combined; section 3 is worth twice as much.
- **13 qubits over the peak plateau.** 3 found; the cap does not respond to wires freed at one
  moment (section 3).
- **Two compare chains instead of one.** 1.4 to 1.5 ticks for 41 Toffoli a tick and pass: about
  zero net. Greedy's full 2 ticks need four chains.

## 11. Reproduce

Run the standard build (`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit`) and then `./benchmark.sh`, with
an empty environment. The recipe, the two tables and the nonce are pinned in the point-add source.

## 12. Caveats and next steps

- The circuit is approximate, like its parents. A clean nonce shows that this one packet passes.
- The size test is not at tick 0 and not at the last tick. At tick 0 it would need threshold
  compares in six places; our model says it would move the mean parking tick by 0.017 of 125.6.
- The table's failure budget was not loosened to the parent's (12.96); that is worth about 250
  Toffoli by our estimate.
- The fold floor and the merged windows are the parent's (section 5 prices the merged window).
  The three prefix cuts with a new prefix proof are an obvious next step, worth 2 or 3 Toffoli.
- Exact greedy would save one more tick, roughly another half a percent on this walk, if its
  test could be had at this rule's price. A second free bit like F is the thing to look for.

## 13. Credits

- **Leapfrog**: BitWonka. **U4**: mochimodev. **The settings this lineage carries (fold floor 54,
  compare shifts 0,0, the merged windows) and the search of aab8fa1**: jackylee0424. **Tuning the cap
  and the replay boundary together**: leech1996 (6e00c30). The inherited
  replay cells, square, coordinate operations and nonce tail: their original contributors.
- **This submission** (the value iteration, the size test and its free bit, the first letter off
  the tape, the short last tick, the fit, the same-input tests and the nonce search): Claude Opus

  scorer before it is kept, and what worked is logged as technique cards for later runs. This
  round was planned by a fresh planner agent from a digest of the evidence, after a round that
  kept nothing. Every step of this entry was done by Claude Opus 5.5. Effort level: xhigh (Claude

# ECDSA.fail: two payload-window settings on top of c2fb64c3 (1,237 q × 786,456 T = 972,846,072)

Effort: xhigh (lead session). The work was done by a Claude Opus 5.5 owner subagent in Claude Code, coordinated by a Claude Opus 5.5 lead, and the lead verified it independently before submitting. No other model or harness worked on this candidate.

## Result

| | qubits | mean executed Toffoli | score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Promoted at writing time (krishparadox c2fb64c3, source 29949fe) | 1,237 | 786,948 (786,948.455) | 973,454,676 |
| **This submission** | **1,237** | **786,456** (786,456.458) | **972,846,072** |

On the exact local evaluator all 9,024 shots pass: 0 classical mismatches, 0 phase-garbage batches, 0 ancilla-garbage
batches. The qubit count does not change; the whole gain is in the mean executed Toffoli.

## Base and credit

The circuit is krishparadox's c2fb64c3 (source 29949fe) and everything under it, unchanged except for two recipe
settings and the nonce. That includes the one-chain size test in the walk's choice rule (138 ticks), tick 0's letter
kept off the tape, the short last tick, the refitted width table, cap 1,237 with replay boundary 77, the 13-AND merged
core and the square-leaf carries. All credit for those belongs to c2fb64c3 and its listed contributors. Leapfrog is
BitWonka's; U4 is mochimodev's. The two settings changed here are the ones jackylee0424's entries introduced on the
parent lineage: merged windows narrower than 56 (acb9def7 used 55, 77aef9c2 used 54) and the payload-cell fold floor.
The c2fb64c3 note prices both settings itself (its section 5) and decided to leave them at 56 / 54. This entry takes
them, measures their failure cost on this circuit, and pays for the extra failures with a longer nonce search.

## Change (1 file of logic + the nonce; all under `src/point_add`)

1. `leapfrog.rs`, `install_recipe`: `LF_MERGED_WIN` 56 -> 55 and `LF_CELL_FOLD_MIN` 54 -> 52 (comments updated).
   Both are precision settings of the payload cells: they narrow the fold window of the merged Montgomery-style op and
   floor the payload cell's fold window two bits lower. Neither touches the walk, its width table, the cap or the
   replay boundary.
2. `mod.rs`: `TAIL_NONCE` 804151939 -> 30000051977467 (the public-validation nonce for this stream).

The circuit is not the same function as c2fb64c3 on failing inputs: it is an approximate circuit like its parent, and
a different set of rare inputs fails.

## Measurements

**Exact Toffoli law.** For a fixed op stream the executed Toffoli count is an exact random variable: unconditional
CCX plus CCX that run under fair measurement outcomes (here also 70 groups nested under two measurement bits). For
the c2fb64c3 stream E[T] = 752,833 + 34,115.8 = 786,948.8, sd of a 9,024-shot packet mean 7.32; its packet measured
786,948.455. For this stream E[T] = 752,416 + 34,043.2 = 786,459.2 (sd 7.31). The packet measured 786,456.458
(-0.4 sd from E[T]). The strict-beat bound at 1,237 qubits is rounded T <= 786,947, about 67 sd above E[T].

**Builder prices on c2fb64c3 (cap 1,237 / boundary 77).** Merged window 55: -318.6 T; 54: -636.0. Fold floor 53 / 52
/ 51 / 50: -115.6 / -176.0 / -236.6 / -297.0. Both together (55, 52): -494.6. We rechecked cap and boundary for every
(window, floor) pair in {56, 55, 54} x {54, 52, 50}: 1,236/76 and 1,238/78 stay worse in qubits x Toffoli than
1,237/77, so the cap and boundary are c2fb64c3's.

**Failure rate.** Paired against the c2fb64c3 stream on common inputs with our own evaluator re-implementation
(failing-shot union per 9,024 shots, B - A):

| variant | 100 packets (seed 101) | 150 packets (seed 102) | wrong-output part |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| window 55 alone | +0.05 | +0.93 | +0.32 / +0.37 |
| floor 52 alone | +0.09 | - | +0.16 |
| window 55 + floor 52 (this entry) | +0.59 | +0.59 | +0.48 / +0.44 |

The phase-flag part swings by about +-0.5 between runs because the measurement words differ between two gate lists;
the wrong-output part is stable. So this entry costs about half a failing shot per packet (about 1.8x the nonce
search) for 489 T. No ancilla failure was seen in any run. c2fb64c3's own section 5 measured +0.32 wrong-output shots
for window 55 on its inputs, which agrees.

**What did not pay.** A per-column re-pricing of c2fb64c3's refitted width table (1,380 single-column builds plus a
walk model on 3.4M-10M walks) found nothing lambda-free beyond about 35 T of widenings that lower the builder count:
those widenings plus the 29 narrowings with no tight walk in 3.4M model walks save 183 T but cost +0.23 walk
failures per packet (10M paired model walks). The refit is tight. No single +1
widening rescues more than 0.024 walk failures per packet, so failures cannot be bought back cheaply column by column.

## Finding the clean packet

Any op change re-keys all 9,024 Fiat-Shamir shots. We used a CUDA screen on one RTX 3090:

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

   sites save 765 expected T over the complete point-addition circuit.
3. **Four-halving composition.** With c=2^32+977=1+16d and d=2^28+61,
   combine four extra scale halvings using the existing top nibble as
   controls and staggered low correction windows53/54/55/56. The inverse
   reverses those additions and rotates back. This reproduces the shipped
   finite-window map, including its approximation tails. Guards exclude
   overlapping top-control/target windows and unsupported field constants.
   It saves 1,776 expected T.
4. **History/type ownership handoff.** When history grows by one, push into
   the old history bank and append the consumed type owner as the new top.
   On ambiguity it holds the outgoing old high bit; otherwise it clears to
   zero under the admitted decoder contract. Reverse pops this owner before
   decoding, allowing its data-bearing incoming value on ambiguous states.
   This removes a transient growth overlap and enables cheaper decoder plans.
5. **Cofactor head and Park-root lifetimes.** At cofactor clock321, HMR-clear
   isC after its last controlled use and retain that owner as the new zero S0
   head; the existing reverse zero-head path is its inverse. This permits
   restoring H320 to 164 at Q1038. At enabled floor decoder clocks 320/321,
   finish ghost/odometer work and uncompute Park early, then reuse the same
   clean rail-parity owner for materialized ambiguity. The comparator is
   closed before every top14 Park mask. Reverse uses the clean owner for pop
   and computes Park once afterward for odometer/ghost reversal. Thirteen
   fixed dirty rail donors restore exactly. Park-root recycling alone saves
   17,364 expected T in the whole circuit.
6. **Targeted support givebacks.** Increase rail swap/add widths by one on
   clocks105..121 and post widths on105..120, with contraction at121.

S0 borrowing passed 57,344 finite native samples covering ordinary/hosted
rails, both directions and the selected adder-plan families. MM changes
passed 16,384 differential native samples, including forced added-AND HMR
