# Failures bought back and sold at a better price: a refit width table, the 22-bit rule window and merged window 55 (1,236 qubits)

| | |
|---|---|
| Built on | jackylee0424's f156900 (972,088,044 = 786,479 T x 1,236 Q), source commit a2325be |
| Score | **971,660,388** = 786,133 T x 1,236 Q (0.044% under f156900) |
| Toffoli (average executed) | 786,132.537 on this packet; 786,219.5 by the builder's expected count |
| Qubits | **1,236** |
| Walk | 138 ticks, unchanged |
| Ground nonce | 1102617946 |
| Failing shots per 9,024 (lambda) | 19.33 +- 0.21 on 473 packets of this gate list's own inputs. On the same 320 packets it has 0.16 +- 0.18 fewer failing shots than f156900 (section 5) |

The build uses the pinned recipe with no environment overrides. All changes are under
`src/point_add`: recipe values in `leapfrog.rs`, one new table file in `leapfrog_data/`, and the
room profile and the nonce constant in `mod.rs`.

## 1. What this entry is

Several recent entries each sold a few tenths of a failing shot for Toffoli: a compare that
starts later, a rule window one bit shorter with 40 hand edits to the width table, a narrower
merged window. We measured every one of those settings on the same test packets, one change at a time,
and found that they do not sell failures at the same price. The width table sells a failing shot
for about 1,000 Toffoli. The shorter rule window sells one for about 480, and the merged window
at 54 for about 530. So this entry buys those two back and sells in the table instead. It ends
with 346 fewer Toffoli than f156900 at a failing-shot count that is not above it.

| Change against f156900 | What it does | Section |
|---|---|---|
| Rule window back to 22 bits (late steps 20, 18, 16, 14, 12) | Buys back about 0.9 failing shots for 438 Toffoli | 2 |
| Merged window 54 back to 55 | Buys back about 0.6 failing shots for 325 Toffoli | 2 |
| The whole width table refit at a looser budget, in place of the 40 edits | Sells about 1.0 failing shot for 994 Toffoli | 3 |
| Room profile picked cell by cell (19 cells) | 180 Toffoli at no measured cost in failures | 4 |

Kept from f156900: cap 1,236 with replay boundary 76, fold floor 50, boundary compare widened by
one bit from tick 120. No tick was removed and no new mechanism was added: this is a better
allocation of the failure budget, found by measurement. Against f156900 it has 346 fewer Toffoli
on the board, and 0.16 +- 0.18 fewer failing shots on 320 shared packets.

## 2. One price list for the failure budget

**Method.** One reference gate list ("A": cap 1,236, boundary 76, merged window 54, fold floor 50,
compare from tick 120, c2fb64c's table, our room profile). Every other gate list is run on A's
test inputs for the same 160 nonces, with the official test logic, shot for shot. That gives a
paired difference in failing shots and in executed Toffoli. Table and window failures show as
wrong outputs, which is the less noisy column; compare failures show as wrong phase.

| Change on A | Toffoli | Failing shots | Toffoli a shot |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boundary compare off | -298 | +0.77 +- 0.17 | 388 |
| Boundary compare from tick 130 instead of 120 | -158 | +0.43 +- 0.23 | about 370 |
| Boundary compare from tick 100 | +209 | -0.25 +- 0.14 | 836 |
| Boundary compare on every tick | +978 | -1.08 +- 0.16 | 905 |
| Both compares widened from tick 120 | +19 | +0.13 +- 0.21 | no gain |
| Merged window 53 | -321 | +1.32 +- 0.09 | 243 |
| Merged window 52 | -635 | +4.05 +- 0.16 | 157 |
| Fold floor 49 | -60 | +0.18 +- 0.03 | 331 |
| Fold floor 48 | -71 | +0.38 +- 0.05 | 190 |
| Fold floor 46 | -89 | +0.67 +- 0.07 | 133 |
| Rule window 21, same table | -438 | +0.92 +- 0.22 | 476 |
| Rule window 20, same table | -874 | +1.75 +- 0.27 | 499 |
| dfb1aec's 40 table edits alone (window 22) | -40 | +0.24 +- 0.04 | |
| Table refit at budget 7.2e-4 | -298 | +0.29 +- 0.04 | 1,013 |
| Table refit at 7.3e-4 | -457 | +0.46 +- 0.05 | 1,002 |
| Table refit at 7.5e-4 | -714 | +0.74 +- 0.07 | 967 |
| Table refit at 7.7e-4 (this entry) | -994 | +1.02 +- 0.08 | 975 |
| Table refit at 8.0e-4 | -1,280 | +1.60 +- 0.10 | 800 (the last step 493) |

And in the other direction, measured on the refit table: merged window 54 to 55 buys 0.61 shots
for 325 Toffoli (533 a shot); 55 to 56 buys 0.39 for 318 (815); fold floor 50 to 52 buys 0.14 for
114 (800).

**Reading.** Sell where a shot is worth 1,000 (the table, up to the 7.7e-4 budget) and buy where
it costs about 500 (the rule window, merged window 55, the late compare). Stop there: the next
table step brings 493 a shot, and the next buys cost 800 (merged window 56, fold floor 52). The
shorter rule window and the narrower merged window or fold floor are sales at 130 to 500 a shot;
this entry undoes two of them and makes none.

**We also tried the shorter rule window with its own refit table** (a fresh 4,000,000-walk sample
under the 21-bit rule, then the same fit). It stays behind: at -575 Toffoli against A it adds
0.92 +- 0.32 failing shots, and at -759 it adds 1.15 +- 0.24, where this entry's 22-bit package
at -669 adds 0.29 +- 0.17. A 20-bit window with its own table is worse again.

**Cap and boundary.** With this table and these settings, cap 1,237 with boundary 77 gives
785,554 x 1,237 = 971,729,803 and cap 1,236 with boundary 76 gives 786,125 x 1,236 = 971,650,747
on the same packets, at the same failing shots. So this entry keeps f156900's cap and boundary
(first used in 61e3b07).

## 3. The table refit

The width table has 138 rows of five widths (the rail after the tick, the three forced adds, the
shift). c2fb64c's table came from a "peel" fit, and this entry runs the same fit with a looser
budget:

1. Simulate 4,000,000 walks under the pinned rule. Keep the per-cell needs of every walk that
   parks in time and comes within a tail level of 3e-4 of any cell (17,766 walks).
2. Start from the cell-wise maximum of those walks. Repeat: lower the cell whose current maximum
   is held by the fewest surviving walks per Toffoli saved, drop those walks, and tighten every
   cell to the survivors' maximum.
3. Stop when the walks dropped plus the walks not parked reach the budget.

c2fb64c used a budget of 7.0e-4 per walk; this table uses 7.7e-4 (1,555 walks dropped where the
old table dropped 1,274). 49 rows change against c2fb64c's table. The walk model predicted +0.9
failing shots a packet for it; the full test measured +1.02 +- 0.08.

**The fit's weights against the builder's own prices.** The fit weighs a bit of rail width at 2
Toffoli, a bit of each forced add at 4 and a bit of the shift at 6, doubled from tick 74. We
priced every cell on the builder (1,237 builds: each cell one bit less and one bit more). The true
prices are far from those weights: a rail-width bit is worth exactly 0 on ticks 6 to 75, the third
forced add is worth 11.3 on average, and on some late rail-width cells one bit less saves nothing
while one bit more costs up to 606. A fit that uses these prices as weights came out 900 Toffoli
worse at the same budget. The price is kinked at the fitted value near the cap, and the fixed
weights do useful work by accident: they lower rail-width cells first, which removes the slow
walks that also hold up the add columns. On this entry's table the best single-cell sale brings
570 Toffoli a failing shot and the cheapest single-cell buy costs 887, so the fit is at a local
optimum for one-cell moves.

dfb1aec's hand edits (kept by f156900) narrow add columns in early rows and widen the rail in
nine late rows. On our draws they save 40 Toffoli and add 0.24 failing shots at a 22-bit window,
so they were doing repair work for the 21-bit window. With the window back at 22 the refit
replaces them.

## 4. The room profile

The inherited switch `HEO_PIN_I35_PROFILE` gives single payload cells one or two wires of extra
carry room. The lineage's profile was tuned for an older cap. We built the circuit with flat room
budgets 0 to 3 with a per-cell census switched on, read each cell's Toffoli at each budget, and
picked per cell. At cap 1,236 and boundary 76 the pick has 19 cells:

`430:1:1,440:0:1,446:0:2,536:1:1,581:1:1,588:1:2,611:1:1,627:1:1,636:0:1,646:1:1,655:1:1,666:0:1,670:0:2,670:1:1,675:0:2,675:1:1,681:0:2,681:1:1,687:1:2`

It saves 180 Toffoli against the inherited profile on 180 paired draws, with no change in failing
shots that we can measure (-0.06 +- 0.15). It is not an exact rewrite: about one shot in 500,000
changes its output. The same census at caps 1,235 and 1,237 and boundaries 75 to 77 chose this cap
and boundary.

## 5. Failure rate and the limiting contract

All three gate lists below were run on the same 320 packets (dfb1aec's own test inputs, nonces
922000000 to 922000319), with the official test logic, shot for shot.

| Gate list | Failing shots a packet | Against dfb1aec | Wrong output against dfb1aec |
|---|---|---|---|
| dfb1aec (the entry before f156900) | 19.22 | | |
| f156900 (rebuilt from its recipe; 786,480 Toffoli here, 786,479 on the board) | 19.68 | +0.46 +- 0.12 | +0.62 +- 0.04 |
| **This entry** | 19.51 | +0.29 +- 0.18 | +0.48 +- 0.15 |

- **Against f156900, packet by packet:** -0.16 +- 0.18 failing shots (wrong output -0.14 +- 0.15).
- **On this gate list's own inputs** (473 packets): 19.33 +- 0.21. The estimate is under the
  lineage's 19.5; the upper end of its error bar (mean + 2 SE = 19.75) is not. By the paired
  figure f156900 would read about 19.5 on the same footing (derived, not measured).
- No ancilla garbage in any run.
- Pairing matters. Two samples of 320 packets on different inputs differ by about 0.35 failing
  shots from noise alone. On shared inputs the standard error of a table change is 0.04.
- **A second gate list of this family is also clean:** the same recipe with the table at 7.5e-4
  and nonce 1002967331 scores 971,987,928 (786,398 x 1,236) and has 0.38 +- 0.18 fewer failing
  shots than f156900 (18.85 +- 0.19 on its own inputs). Both nonces were found within 20
  minutes of each other on 9 October; we send the better score.

The contract carried by this lineage asks that Lambda stay below 19.5 and that an error trade be
offset by a better one. This entry is an offset of that kind: it undoes two trades (the 21-bit
rule window at about 480 Toffoli a shot, merged window 54 at about 530) and makes a better one
(the table, at about 1,000 a shot), and it ends at or below its parent in failing shots. The
notices are copied in full at the end.

## 6. Nonce search

- **Stage 0** is an integer model of the walk that reads the same table and anchors as the builder
  and rejects a nonce at its first shot whose walk leaves the table. On 113 full packets of this
  gate list it never rejected a shot that passes the full test.
- **On a GPU.** We ported stage 0 to CUDA inside the kernel of Jieyi Long's public
  `ecdsafail_gpu_toolkit` (MIT licence): its field, curve, hash and per-nonce derivation are used
  as they are; its filter is replaced by ours. The port was held to our CPU tool before use:
  16,000,000 random walks on four tables with 0 differences, every denominator and every stage-0
  record of 18 full packets equal, and the rejecting shot equal on 1,000,000 nonces across four
  gate lists. One RTX 3090 scans about 10,400 nonces a second; 22 CPU threads add about 4,200.
- A nonce kept by stage 0 goes to the CPU for the full official test logic on all 9,024 shots.
  Only that prints a find.
- **This search:** about 35 million nonces: 32 million on the GPU in two runs and 2,630,429 on
  the CPU. Stage 0 kept 2 on the CPU; the second passed the full test. At 19.33 failing shots the
  expected number of tries is about 250 million, so this find came early (a chance of about
  13%). The CPU search's audit: 517 of 517 sampled stage-0 rejects fail the full test at the
  flagged shot.

## 7. Reproduce

`git checkout a2325be`, apply this submission's `src/point_add`, run `./benchmark.sh`. It prints
"all 9024 shots OK", 786132.537 average executed Toffoli and 1236 qubits.
SHA-256 of `ops.bin`: `920646c1ea181300743632202c74a5ffc2bdc4a71a78b550c90bde321dfdc4aa`.

- The price list is 160 packets a row. A row's failing-shot figure carries about +-0.15, or

GCD Skywalk, by Matt Zweil

Credit: Matt Zweil & MAI-A.A.E. (Autonomous AI Entity)
AI Coding Models: Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable, OpenAI GPT-6

This work was sponsored by the Mochimo Foundation.
Mochimo is the world's first fully post-quantum secure cryptocurrency. Mainnet since June 25, 2018.
Join us on Discord: https://discord.mochimo.org/

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

# froghop-single: a one-hop packed Euclid for low-qubit secp256k1 point addition (940 qubits, 8.74M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code. The initial design ("PX") came out of a Claude Opus
research sub-agent; the gate-level build, schedule fit and point-add integration were done in the main session.
**Result (official `ecdsafail run`, all 9024 shots OK):** 940 qubits × 8,738,261 average executed Toffoli =
**8,213,965,340**. Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point.
**Base:** a new `src/point_add` (the froghop inversion core in `froghop_single.rs` plus its own point-add shell); harness
unchanged.
**Name:** froghop-single makes **one hop per Euclid step**: one up-and-down excursion of the divisor register.

## ELI5

**The job:** turn dx into 1/dx (twice per point addition) using as few qubits as possible. Euclid does it by
repeated division:
- the **remainders** shrink every step, from 256 bits down to 1;
- a **receipt** (the Bezout cofactor) grows every step, and at the end it is the answer.

Because one shrinks while the other grows, they can **share one shelf**. Each register holds a remainder at one end
and a receipt at the other, with a **dividing line** in between. That saves almost half the qubits.

The catch: the dividing line sits in a different place on every shot. If you track it per shot, every operation
has to check, lane by lane, which side of the line it is on. That checking is what makes the classic shared-shelf
designs expensive. (Luo et al.'s EEA already fixes the order of its steps; froghop-single also fixes where the line is.)

**froghop-single's difference:** the dividing line moves on a **fixed timetable** that is the same for every shot, with
enough slack that every shot's numbers fit on their own side. Nothing ever checks the line, so every operation
runs on fixed wires. A second trick: each Euclid step has some catch-up work (finishing the receipt from the last
division) and some look-ahead work (lining up the next division). froghop-single does both in the same trip up the
register, then divides on the way back down: **one hop (one round trip) per step** instead of three passes.

| design (module in its code) | how the inversion stores its state | qubits | average Toffoli |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Luo et al. fixed-schedule EEA** (`paper2607_eea`) | remainder + cofactor packed in 259-wire work registers; the steps follow a fixed schedule, the line is tracked per shot in length registers | 792–795 | 301M–574M |
| **Shrunken-PZ** (`shrunken_pz`) | packed Proos–Zalka prefix | 838 | 22.0M |
| **SkyCof** (`skycof`, Skywalk cofactor walk) | binary-GCD rails, each rail sharing a register with its cofactor | 1008–1038 | 2.9M–9.6M |
| **froghop-single** (`froghop_single.rs`) | full-quotient Euclid, remainder + cofactor packed; the line's position follows a fixed classical schedule (`sched.txt`), no masks | **940** | **8.74M** |

froghop-single sits between them: ~70–100 fewer qubits than SkyCof, and 2.5–65× fewer Toffoli than the 792–838 entries.
It pays ~110 qubits of slack (2 × 314 lanes instead of ~2 × 259) to skip every boundary check. On the board it
beats every graded point from 973 to 1011 qubits on both axes.

## 1. Why another packed Euclid

A packed extended Euclid on (p, x') stores (r, t) pairs in shared registers and is history-free: each quotient bit
can be erased from the cofactors alone. froghop-single keeps that, but makes two changes: the register boundary follows a
classical schedule, so no ladder works around a per-shot boundary, and the cofactor update of one step and the
alignment of the next share a single pass.

## 2. The slot

**State.** Cross pairing: dividend register D = (r_{i−1}, t_i), divisor register V = (r_i, t_{i−1}), both W = 314
lanes. Cofactor in wires [0, M), remainder in [M, W), same bit orientation. M(σ) is a classical per-slot schedule;
moving it is a free wire relabel, because the top wire is always a zero gap. V sits rotated against D by a
counter π. The input is x' = min(dx, p − dx).

**One hop per Euclid step.** With cross pairing, the cofactor update of step i−1 (bottom-up, so each
quotient bit can be erased) and the alignment search of step i need the same shift of V against D. So one up-ramp
carries both, and the down-ramp runs the restoring division of step i, pushing quotient bits onto a 24-deep stack:

1. **OUT (up):** pop bit b, apply td += b·(tv ≪ π), erase b with [td ≥ tv ≪ π]; test the alignment
   [R ≥ rv ≪ π]; move up or turn.
2. **RET / DIV (down):** c = [R ≥ rv ≪ π]; R −= c·(rv ≪ π); push c. At π = 0, swap D and V and apply the new
   quotient's bit 0 in the same slot.

That is ~2.4–2.55 slots per quotient bit in our model; 900 fixed slots per traversal.

**Reversibility.** Each decision is recoverable from the post-slot state:
- division bits through the stack and the bottom-up compare (needs t_{i−2} < t_{i−1}, which the reflection
  guarantees);
- moves through the phase;
- "turn vs return" through one extra compare wired one position higher;
- first-step and finished flags through zero tests and a frozen-slot counter.

**Cost per slot (~1,840 Toffoli):**

| part | Toffoli |
|---|---|
| remainder ladder (3 T/lane) | ~437 |
| cofactor ladder with mid-ladder erasure (3 T/lane) | ~505 |
| turn discriminator (top 96 lanes, 2 T/lane) | ~192 |
| V rotation | ~312 |
| step-end D/V swap | ~314 |
| stack, counters, phase | ~90 |

Per traversal ~1.66M T; 4 traversals plus products (~280k per product, ~313k per MAC) give 8.74M.

## 3. Key ideas beyond the slot

- **Fixed boundary schedule:** the r/t boundary of both registers follows `sched.txt`. Every ladder runs on fixed
  wires, with no per-lane decode. W = 314 is fitted to 200k simulated shots.
- **Shared up-ramp:** the previous step's cofactor update and the next step's alignment share one excursion.
- **Two-way rotation (10.25M → 8.74M against our first build):** finished shots oscillate π (+1 on even slots, −1 on odd), so
  the V move is a free relabel by −1 plus a controlled rotate-by-2 (W − 2 instead of 1.5W; −157 T per slot).
- **Short discriminator:** the turn compare reads only the top 96 cofactor lanes (exact unless the relative gap is
  below ~2^-46).

The point addition shell is the measurement-based one: division 1 gives λ = dy/dx; dy is measured away (Hmr) and
its phase fixed by recomputing λ·dx; dx' = λ² − dx − 3·ox; ndy = −λ·dx'; λ is measured away; division 2 recomputes
λ to fix its phase. Products use double-and-add with folding by p = 2^256 − (2^32 + 977) and 32-lane truncated
carry headroom.

## 4. Failure budget

Expected failing shots per 9024-shot run, measured on fresh builds:
- register-width tail from rare large quotients: ~0.3;
- stack depth 24: ~0.1;
- slot count, first-step window, truncations: ~0.05.

Total λ ≈ 0.45. A local diagnostic replays the Fiat–Shamir shot generation from `ops.bin` and checks every division
against every limit; this build passes all 9024 shots. (A first W = 308 schedule fitted to 30k shots failed one shot
in a full run; refitting on 200k shots gave W = 314.)

**Limiting contract.** The PR 419 limiting contract (copied in full in §7) caps a circuit's λ at 18 on 9,024 shots
and rules out trading error directly for score (e.g. round reductions). froghop-single meets it:
- λ ≈ 0.45, about 40× below the cap;
- its only approximations, the 32-lane product carry headroom and the 96-lane turn discriminator, contribute under
  0.05 together;
- the width W and the stack depth are sized for rare inputs, not trimmed for Toffoli.

## 5. Reproduce

`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit` (or `./benchmark.sh`). The boundary schedule is
`src/point_add/sched.txt`; the design note is `src/point_add/memory/FROGHOP_SINGLE.md`. `cargo test --release --bin
build_circuit` runs the gate-level traversal against the integer reference model (`refmodel.rs`) at every slot,
forward + inverse on 384 inputs, and the end-to-end point addition on 64 random point pairs.

## 6. Credits

Register sharing and the history-free packed Euclid follow Luo et al.'s fixed-schedule EEA (arXiv:2607.13816), as
used by gnuchev and bulengerk in the Q792–Q795 entries; the bottom-up cofactor erasure of quotient bits is that
mechanism.
froghop-single's cross pairing, fixed boundary schedule, shared up-ramp and slot machine are by Claude Opus 5.5 in
Claude Code (design sub-agent + main session), working with BitWonka. No reference step code was copied.

# froghop-double: a two-hop exact-packed Euclid for low-qubit secp256k1 point addition (836 qubits, 15.9M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code (main session).
**Result (official `ecdsafail run`, all 9024 shots OK):** 836 qubits × 15,933,765 average executed Toffoli =
**13,320,627,540**. Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point.
**Base:** a new `src/point_add` (the inversion core in `froghop_double.rs`, masked ladders in `mask.rs`, lean
modular products in `modp_double.rs`, plus its own point-add shell); harness unchanged.
**Name:** froghop-double makes **two hops per Euclid step**: up to align, down to divide, up to update the cofactor,
back down. Its sibling froghop-single (940 qubits × 8.74M) makes one.

## ELI5

**The job:** turn dx into 1/dx (twice per point addition) using as few qubits as possible. Euclid does it by
repeated division:
- the **remainders** shrink every step, from 256 bits down to 1;
- a **receipt** (the Bezout cofactor) grows every step, and at the end it is the answer.

Because one shrinks while the other grows, they can **share one shelf**: each register holds a remainder and a
receipt, with a **dividing line** between them.

froghop-single moves that line on a fixed timetable, the same for every shot, so nothing ever checks it. The price
is slack: the shelf has to fit the worst shot at every step, ~110 extra qubits.

**froghop-double's difference:** it packs every shot **exactly**. The remainder grows up from one end of the shelf
and the receipt grows down from the other, like two books pushed to opposite ends: both stay put and only the gap
between them moves. So each register needs just one lane more than the information bound (258), and the line is
checked only inside a narrow window on each step, where it can actually be. The price: with the two numbers facing
opposite ways, the catch-up work (finishing the receipt) and the look-ahead work (lining up the next division) can
no longer share a trip, so each step takes **two hops** instead of one, about twice froghop-single's Toffoli.

| design (module in its code) | how the inversion stores its state | qubits | average Toffoli |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Luo et al. fixed-schedule EEA** (`paper2607_eea`) | remainder + cofactor packed in 259-wire work registers; the steps follow a fixed schedule, the line is tracked per shot in length registers | 792–795 | 301M–574M |
| **froghop-double** (`froghop_double.rs`) | remainder from one end, cofactor from the other, exact per-shot line; checked only inside per-step windows | **836** | **15.9M** |
| **Shrunken-PZ** (`shrunken_pz`) | packed Proos–Zalka prefix | 838 | 22.0M |
| **froghop-single** (`froghop_single.rs`) | the line follows a fixed timetable, never checked; ~110 qubits of slack | 940 | 8.74M |
| **SkyCof** (`skycof`, Skywalk cofactor walk) | binary-GCD rails, each rail sharing a register with its cofactor | 1008–1038 | 2.9M–9.6M |

On the board froghop-double beats the 838-qubit point on both axes, and uses 3.9–36× fewer Toffoli than every graded
point below 836 qubits.

## 1. Why a second froghop

froghop-single's fixed boundary pays for the spread of progress across shots: its registers are 314 lanes wide where
an exact per-shot packing needs 258. froghop-double takes the exact packing (layout after gnuchev's packed-inversion
notes) and keeps the masking cheap by confining it to classical per-slot windows.

## 2. The slot

**State.** Cross pairing as in froghop-single: D = (r_{j−1}, t_j), V = (r_j, t_{j−1}), V rotated against D by π and
hopping ±1 lane per slot. In each W = 258 register the value has its LSB at lane 0 and the cofactor its LSB at lane
W − 1, growing down, so only the boundary floats. The information bound is bl(r_j) + bl(t_{j+1}) ≤ 257; D needs 258
for the first divide slot.

**Two hops per Euclid step.** The reversed orientation shifts the cofactor the opposite way from the value, so
alignment and cofactor update cannot share a ramp. Each step is a 4-phase machine:
1. **AL** (π = 1 .. k+1): compare to find the quotient's length;
2. **DV** (π = k .. 0): restoring division, quotient bits pushed onto a 24-deep stack;
3. **CO** (π = 1 .. k): pop each bit and apply it to the cofactor, erasing it mid-ladder;
4. **RT** (back to 0), then swap the roles of D and V.

1,240 slots per traversal, ~7.8 slots per Euclid step on average.

**One shared boundary register b** (8 bits): bits of the dividend during AL, set to bits of the divisor at the turn
by a one-hot probe, erased by a second probe. Every mask (value side and cofactor side) derives from b, π and the
phase.

**Cost per slot (~2,800 Toffoli):** masked value and cofactor ladders, the turn probes, the CO→RT discriminator
(truncated to 20 lanes below the slot's lowest boundary), rotation and swap. Masking is ~900 T of it, swap and
rotation ~560 T.

## 3. Key ideas beyond the slot

- **Exact per-shot packing:** W = 258, one lane above the information bound, instead of froghop-single's 314.
- **Masks only where the line can be:** running-carry masked cells (bulengerk's "mask the carry transition"), one
  running mask toggled by incremental one-hot decoders inside classical per-slot windows, with comparators fixing
  its start and end.
- **Late source:** the discriminator uses the lane holding rv's always-1 most significant bit as the 0 it stands
  for, which is what lets the q = 1 case fit W = 258.
- **Lean product fold:** the products fold an overflow back as + (2^32 + 977) through 23 clean and 9
  dirty-borrowed headroom lanes, so the product phases fit under the same 836 peak.

The point addition shell is the measurement-based one: division 1 gives λ = dy/dx; dy is measured away (Hmr) and
its phase fixed by recomputing λ·dx; dx' = λ² − dx − 3·ox; ndy = −λ·dx'; λ is measured away; division 2 recomputes
λ to fix its phase.

## 4. Failure budget

The per-slot windows come from a 1.2M-shot raw envelope with a per-window time-shift envelope and margins. Model λ ≈
0.77 expected failing shots per 9024-shot run:
- quotients ≥ 2^25 overflowing the 24-deep stack: ~0.12;
- the window margins and the 20-lane discriminator truncation: the rest.

This build (`NONCE = 1`) passes all 9024 shots.

**Limiting contract.** The PR 419 limiting contract (copied in full in §7) caps a circuit's λ at 18 on 9,024 shots
and rules out trading error directly for score. froghop-double does not build on that circuit and stays far under the
cap at λ ≈ 0.77. For transparency: its window margins and the 20-lane discriminator truncation were tightened from a
λ ≈ 0.12 schedule (836 × 17,173,499) to this one, for 7.2% fewer Toffoli at the same 836 qubits.

## 5. Reproduce

`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit` (or `./benchmark.sh`). The per-slot windows are
`src/point_add/sched_double.txt`; the design note is `src/point_add/memory/FROGHOP_DOUBLE.md`. `cargo test --release
--bin build_circuit` runs the masked-ladder units, the gate-level traversal against the integer reference model
(`refmodel_double.rs`) at every slot, forward + inverse identity, the fold test, and a 64-shot end-to-end point
addition.

## 6. Credits

Register sharing and the history-free packed Euclid follow Luo et al.'s fixed-schedule EEA (arXiv:2607.13816); the
exact-packed layout follows gnuchev's packed-inversion notes; the masked carry cells are bulengerk's "mask the carry
transition". froghop-double's two-hop machine, shared boundary register, windowed masks and late-source
discriminator are by Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, working with BitWonka. No reference step code was copied.

GCD Skywalk, by Matt Zweil

Credit: Matt Zweil & MAI-A.A.E. (Autonomous AI Entity)
AI Coding Models: Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable, OpenAI GPT-6

This work was sponsored by the Mochimo Foundation.
Mochimo is the world's first fully post-quantum secure cryptocurrency. Mainnet since June 25, 2018.
Join us on Discord: https://discord.mochimo.org/

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

# froghop-double: quotient bits in the register gap and lean bookkeeping (836 → 799 qubits, 17.4M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code (main session).
**Result (official `ecdsafail run`, all 9024 shots OK):** 799 qubits × 17,366,577 average executed Toffoli =
**13,875,895,023**. Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point.
**Base:** froghop-double (two hops per Euclid step, exact packing), unchanged as a machine; this submission changes
only its control and scratch bookkeeping. Harness unchanged.

## ELI5

froghop-double already packs each remainder and its receipt (the Bezout cofactor) exactly into two shared shelves
of 258 lanes. Those two shelves plus the other coordinate dy are 772 qubits, and in froghop-double another 64 went
to **bookkeeping**: a stack for quotient bits, a finished-shot counter, the boundary position, phase flags and
scratch.

**This optimization** cuts the bookkeeping from 64 to 27 qubits.
- The biggest item, the 24-slot stack of quotient bits, goes away: the bits are written into the empty gap between
  the two numbers on the shelf, which exists anyway.
- The finished-shot counter moves into shelf lanes whose content is known once a shot is done.
- The rest is tighter encodings: a 6-bit offset instead of an 8-bit boundary, a 3-bit phase code instead of four
  flags, and decoders that borrow idle qubits from dy instead of holding their own.

The price is ~9% more Toffoli: the leaner decoders and the gap-resident stack take a little more work per slot.

## 1. Where the 37 qubits went (836 → 799)

| item | froghop-double (836) | this build (799) |
|---|---|---|
| registers D, V (2 × 258) + dy (256) | 772 | 772 |
| quotient-bit stack (shared with the finished-shot counter) | 24 | 0 |
| boundary register | 8 (b) | 6 (offset u) |
| phase | 4 flags | 3-bit code |
| rotation counter π, depth, reflection bit | 11 | 11 |
| scratch pool | 17 | 7 |
| **total** | **836** | **799** |

The first row alone is 772; with the 20 persistent control qubits it is 792, so this machine bottoms out near 795.
The 799 peak is all-in: the product phases stay at or under 790.

## 2. How

- **Quotient bits in V's gap.** The divide pushes each quotient bit into V-frame lane b + j, inside the gap between
  V's value and cofactor; the top bit is never stored. One merged push/pop swap scan works at physical lane
  (b − 1) + depth + π. This removes the 24-qubit stack.
- **Finished-shot counter in D's top lanes.** Once a shot is done, D holds (1, p), so p's known top bits can carry
  the counter.
- **6-bit offset boundary.** The boundary is stored as u = (b − 1) − base(σ), where base(σ) is a classical
  per-slot column (the running minimum of that slot's boundary values); every value stays below base + 64. It is
  re-centred at the end of each slot.
- **3-bit phase code** p0 p1 p2: AL 001, DV 010, CO 011, RT 000, DONE 100.
- **Moving bit in p2.** Divide and cofactor shots keep the bit being moved (division bit to the push, popped bit to
  the cofactor ladder) in p2; finished shots park their p2 in depth bit 0. So p2 is directly the ladders' write
  gate. The CO→RT flag also lives in p2, and the CO depth decrement is deferred to the top of the cofactor ladder.
- **Conditionally clean decoder levels.** The turn probes' top decoder levels live in depth bits 0..3, which are
  |0⟩ for every turning AL shot.
- **Limited-prefix decoders and borrowed-dirty MCX.** Decoders hold only their top prefix levels; the rest is a
  clean AND chain followed by a Barenco multi-controlled X on borrowed dy qubits. Increments use n − 2 ancillas.
- **Lean product fold:** 10 low lanes plus two 32-lane borrowed-dirty increments.

## 3. Cost

The traversal goes from 3.45M to 3.70M Toffoli per pass. Most of it is the turn discriminator (+62 T per slot from
four instead of five held decoder prefixes) and the value ladder (+41 T per slot from the prefix split where windows
overlap). Four traversals plus products: 15.93M → 17.37M average Toffoli.

The point addition shell, the slot machine, the masked ladders and the late-source discriminator are froghop-double's,
unchanged (see the froghop-double note).

## 4. Failure budget

The per-slot windows come from 1.2M-shot raw extremes (including the push/pop scan window), a per-window envelope
and the base column. Model λ ≈ 0.65 expected failing shots per 9024-shot run. This build (`NONCE = 1`) passes all
9024 shots.

**Limiting contract.** The PR 419 limiting contract (copied in full in §6) caps a circuit's λ at 18 on 9,024 shots
and rules out trading error directly for score. This submission does not build on that circuit and stays far under
the cap at λ ≈ 0.65. It keeps froghop-double's tightened window margins and 20-lane discriminator truncation; the
froghop-double note discloses that trade.

every slot, forward + inverse identity, the fold test, and a 64-shot end-to-end point addition.

# frogdrop: a 3-of-4 Euclid for low-qubit secp256k1 point addition (776 qubits, 188M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code (main session).
**Result (official `ecdsafail run`, all 9024 shots OK):** 776 qubits × 188,053,328 average executed Toffoli =
**145,929,382,528**. Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point.
**Base:** a new `src/point_add` (the inversion core in `frogdrop.rs` and `frogdrop_col.rs`, the column schedule in
`sched_frogdrop.txt`, lean modular products in `modp_frogdrop.rs`, plus its own point-add shell); harness unchanged.
**Name:** frogdrop **drops** one of the four Euclid values: it holds three and rebuilds the fourth every step.

## ELI5

**The job:** turn dx into 1/dx (twice per point addition) using as few qubits as possible. Euclid does it with four
numbers that change every step:
- two **remainders**, which shrink from 256 bits down to 1;
- two **receipts** (the Bezout cofactors), which grow, and at the end one of them is the answer.

The froghops keep all four, packed two to a shelf.

**frogdrop's difference:** it keeps only **three**. The four are tied by one equation, r_{j−1}·t_j + r_j·t_{j−1} = p,
so any three give back the fourth. Each step frogdrop rebuilds the missing one with a multiply and a divide, takes the
Euclid step, and drops a different one.
- The values need 426 qubits instead of 516 (a 288-lane ring plus a 138-lane register, against froghop-double's two
  258-lane shelves).
- The rebuild needs more control and scratch (94 qubits against 27), so the net saving is 23 qubits.
- The price is Toffoli: the multiply and divide run on every step, about 11× froghop-double's cost.

| design (module in its code) | how the inversion stores its state | qubits | average Toffoli |
|---|---|---|---|
| **frogdrop** (`frogdrop.rs`) | three of the four values; the fourth rebuilt every step by a 2-adic multiply and divide | **776** | **188M** |
| **Luo et al. fixed-schedule EEA** (`paper2607_eea`) | remainder + cofactor packed in 259-wire work registers; the steps follow a fixed schedule, the line is tracked per shot in length registers | 792–795 | 301M–671M |
| **froghop-double, lean bookkeeping** (`froghop_double.rs`) | all four, exactly packed in two 258-lane shelves; 27 qubits of bookkeeping | 799 | 17.4M |
| **froghop-double** (`froghop_double.rs`) | the same shelves; 64 qubits of bookkeeping | 836 | 15.9M |

On the board frogdrop would be the lowest-qubit graded point (the lowest today is 792), and it beats every graded
point from 792 to 796 qubits on both axes.

## 1. The state: three of four

Extended Euclid on (p, dx): r_{j+1} = r_{j−1} − q r_j, t_{j+1} = t_{j−1} + q t_j, with the invariant

    r_{j-1} t_j + r_j t_{j-1} = p.

The traversal stores three values and recovers the dropped one each step with an exact in-place 2-adic map

    Z <- (p - Z X) / Y

(multiply by X, subtract from p, divide by Y; every operation is mod 2^L on a per-shot region, exact because the true
quotient is an integer that fits). Two phases:
- **HR** (early): hold Z = r_j, X = t_{j−1}, Y = t_j (the big remainder lives in the ring, the small cofactors in Q).
- **HT** (late): hold Z = t_j, X = r_{j−1}, Y = r_j.

Each shot switches HR → HT once, at its first HR state with bl(r_j) ≤ 118. The switch is a non-stepping column that
reuses the column's own map with the operands exchanged (HR(j) ↔ HT(j) is direction-agnostic). With nq = 138 the Q
register's need has a hard edge at 256 − 118 and a ~1e-6 tail from a huge quotient at the switch.

The traversal runs Euclid on dx itself, with no reflection below p/2. The only place where the HR sign trick could see
T = t is column 1 (j = 2 with q_1 = 1), where the sign of T − 1 − bq·t is read instead.

## 2. Layout (776 qubits)

| register | qubits | role |
|---|---|---|
| dy (passenger) | 256 | also the borrowed (dirty) pool for every carry chain |
| ring | 288 | Z at the bottom (LSB lane 0), the top pair value reversed at the top; ≥ 31-lane gap |
| Q | 138 | the other pair value (the map's X at column start) |
| sy, sx | 18 | bl(top value), spare size register (they alternate roles each column) |
| ph, idle counter | 8 | phase; 7-bit counter (0 while stepping, 1 + idle columns once finished) |
| column scratch pool | 68 | carved per column; roles overlap only across disjoint stages |

Product phase: x/inverse 256 + y 256 + z 256 + 2 (adder carry + fold flag) + 6 (counter) = 776. The inverse's
magnitude t_{N−1} ≤ p/2 < 2^255 leaves its lane 255 free, which holds the counter's top bit during the products.

## 3. One column (every shot, lockstep: one Euclid step, a switch, or idle)

1. Probe sz = bl(Z); compute the switch flag.
2. **Masked swap** (ring lane l ↔ Q[n−1−l] for l ≥ sz + h, per shot) brings Y into Q.
3. **Streaming quotient estimate P.** Rotate the ring so Z's top K = 29 bits sit at a fixed top, and rotate Q by sy
   so Y's top KP = 30 bits sit at Q's top lanes. Then a restoring division of an all-ones dividend by Zh = Z_hi | 1
   is streamed MSB-first into a second restoring division by Yh; only the last QB = 24 steps compare. Reciprocal
   bits are recovered from the remainder's parity, so the reciprocal is never stored. Outputs: q0 (24 bits) and rho
   (31 bits); the reciprocal's remainder lives in the ring gap. The pipeline start is gated per shot.
4. **Middle (one code path for HR, HT, switching and idle shots):**
   - HR: bq = [rho < Xh]; T −= bq·t; bq ^= sign (T < t, so the sign is exactly bq); T += q0·t.
   - HT: R −= q0·r in the same q0 pass through the complement trick ~(~R + q0·r); bq = sign; R += bq·r;
     bq ^= [rho < Xh(R′)].
   - Switching and finished shots have their q0 controls gated off.

   The ladder is capped at nq + 1 lanes (every pair value fits Q); wide-region shots read the sign at the ladder top
   through one comparator.
5. Undo P, swap back, erase sz.
6. **Map stage:** probe sx = bl(X), order the sizes, map with cut = n − max(bl X, bl Y). The map is v2 alignment
   (rotate Q to X_odd, shift Z's region), multiply by X in a rotated frame (the ring rotated so the region sits under
   a fixed top, controls gated by a decoder of the per-shot boundary), p − Z, masked swap, divide by Y_odd in the
   frame, shift down.
7. Switch exchange, phase flip, idle counter.

## 4. Key ideas beyond the column

- **Three values, one map.** The same 2-adic map does the step, the HR → HT switch and the idle moves.
- **The reciprocal is never stored:** the two divisions are streamed into each other and the reciprocal's bits are
  read back from the remainder's parity.
- **Sign tricks instead of a correction register:** in HR the sign of T − bq·t is exactly bq, and HT uses
  ~(~R + q0·r), so the off-by-one correction costs no stored bit.
- **p − Z X needs no +2^256 term** (Z X ≤ p keeps the high lanes zero), and every carry chain uses dy as a borrowed
  (dirty) pool.
- **Idle without a done flag.** Finished shots idle with q = 0 maps, alternating A0 = (t_{N−1}, R, 1) and
  B0 = (t_{N−2}, 1, R). The four maps (q = 0 map, switch, their product, identity) form a Klein four-group, so a
  one-column identity is impossible; the 7-bit counter makes the done transition reversible, and "done" is simply
  counter ≠ 0. At the end, one map controlled by the counter's parity brings every shot to A0, and a last map-free HT
  middle with Y = 1 clears R. The inverse is ±t_{N−1}, with the sign (−1)^N read off the counter's parity and the
  column count, and applied to the product, not to the inverse.
- **Lean product fold:** the modular products' constant fold (+c = 2^32 + 977) uses signed-digit (NAF) controlled
  increments on borrowed qubits, so the product phase needs only 2 clean scratch qubits.

The point addition shell is froghop-double's measurement-based one: two divisions, with dy and λ measured away and
their phases fixed later against a recomputed value.

## 5. Cost and schedule

About 46M Toffoli per traversal, of which the map is ~60%. Four traversals plus the products: 188.05M average.

203 columns. Per-column classical envelopes (size ranges of Z and Y, the map's cut range, the switch lanes, which
column kinds occur) come from 1M sampled shots per kind. They are smoothed over ±4 columns, widened by 4 bits, and the
kind windows are extended by 6 columns. Validated on 2M fresh shots: 0 envelope misses.

## 6. Failure budget

Failures are classical predicates of the two traversal inputs:
- the switch map's region (the switch multiplies t_{j−1} by r_j inside n − bl(t_j) lanes; an even r_j with both
  cofactors near 138 bits overflows it): ~1.4e-5 per input;
- a quotient ≥ 2^24: ~1e-5;
- a windowed estimate off by one, e > TOT, Q need > 138, an envelope miss: a few 1e-6 each.

Carry tails are truncated at 40 lanes. Total ~3.5e-5 per input: model λ ≈ 0.63 expected failing shots per 9024-shot
run. A predictor that hashes the op stream like eval_circuit and checks every shot's two traversal inputs picks the
nonce. It was checked on a real failure: an earlier 778-qubit build failed the official check on exactly one shot at
nonce 0, and the predictor flagged that same shot (a switch-map overflow). This build (nonce 4) is predicted clean
and passes all 9024 shots. The nonce is a single X X pair on a chosen qubit, so the op count stays fixed.

**Limiting contract.** The PR 419 limiting contract (copied in full in §9) caps a circuit's λ at 18 on 9,024 shots
and rules out trading error directly for score. frogdrop does not build on that circuit and stays far under the cap
at λ ≈ 0.63.

## 7. Reproduce

`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit` (or `./benchmark.sh`). The column envelopes are
`src/point_add/sched_frogdrop.txt`. The circuit is large: 638,940,473 ops, `ops.bin` is 1.66 GB on disk, and the
local `eval_circuit` takes ~6 minutes and ~36 GB of memory. `cargo test --release --bin build_circuit` runs the
primitive and masked-ladder units, a full traversal against an integer model, the real 203-column schedule on 64
shots, the fold test, and a 64-shot end-to-end point addition (0 mismatches, phase 0, all ancillas clean). The
schedule generator (`frogdrop_sched_gen`) and the nonce predictor (`frogdrop_predict_nonce`) are `#[ignore]` tests,
run with `--ignored` and `FROGDROP_*` settings.

## 8. Credits

The 3-of-4 Euclid state idea follows the packed / space-efficient extended-Euclid line (Luo et al.; gnuchev's Q810 and
bulengerk's Q792 lineage). Measurement-based uncomputation of dy and λ follows Luo et al. and gnuchev. krishparadox's
1,237-qubit Leapfrog entry, which measures tick 0's letter early and makes it again at the end, informed the
scratch-budget exploration. frogdrop's
three-value state, 2-adic map, streaming estimate, lockstep columns and idle machinery are by Claude Opus 5.5 in
Claude Code, working with BitWonka. No reference step code was copied.

## 9. PR 419 limiting contract

# frogdrop: an ancilla-free modular adder and 8-bit size registers (776 → 775 qubits, 185.8M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code (main session).
**Result (official `ecdsafail run`, all 9024 shots OK):** 775 qubits × 185,798,744 average executed Toffoli =
**143,994,026,600**. Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point.
**Base:** frogdrop (776 × 188,053,328), unchanged as a machine; this submission changes its modular arithmetic and
the width of two size registers. Harness unchanged.

## ELI5

frogdrop's qubit count is set by two moments that both sat at 776:
- **the traversal** (the Euclid walk that turns dx into 1/dx);
- **the products inside each division** (1/dx times dy), while the walk's idle counter is still alive.

This build takes one qubit off each, so the whole circuit drops to 775.
- **Products:** every modular add needed two clean helper qubits, a carry-in and an overflow flag. A ripple adder
  that needs no carry-in removes the first one.
- **Traversal:** two size registers were 9 bits wide, but they only ever hold the sizes of the small pair values
  (at most 138 bits), so 8 bits suffice. One of them doubles as scratch for the quotient estimate, which takes one
  pool qubit back: net one qubit.

Toffoli also goes down slightly (188.05M → 185.80M): the new adder is a little cheaper, and the narrower register
skips some decoder steps.

## 1. Where the qubit went

| phase | item | frogdrop (776) | this build (775) |
|---|---|---|---|
| traversal | size registers sy, sx | 18 | 16 |
| traversal | column scratch pool | 68 | 69 |
| traversal | dy 256, ring 288, Q 138, phase 1, counter 7 | 690 | 690 |
| | **traversal total** | **776** | **775** |
| products | inverse 256, dy 256, product 256 | 768 | 768 |
| products | idle counter (its top bit parked in the inverse's free lane 255) | 6 | 6 |
| products | modular-arithmetic scratch | 2 (carry-in, flag) | 1 (flag) |
| | **products total** | **776** | **775** |

## 2. How

**Ancilla-free controlled add.** z += ctl·y (mod 2^256) uses the Takahashi–Tani–Kunihiro ripple: a CNOT cascade
stores the carries in the addend's own lanes, so no carry-in qubit exists. For the controlled version the carry
computation runs unconditionally and only the n CNOTs that write sum bits become Toffolis controlled by ctl:
3n − 2 Toffoli, against ~3n for the controlled Cuccaro ladder it replaces. With ctl = 0 the second half is exactly
the inverse of the first.

**Exact overflow flag.** The flag k = ctl ∧ carry_out(z + y) is taken inside the same ripple: one Toffoli on the
addend's top lane before the cascade, and one 3-control Toffoli after the carry chain (4 Toffoli on a borrowed
qubit). The adder, its controlled form and the flag were checked exhaustively for n ≤ 6, and the 256-bit modular add
and product on random and carry-heavy operands.

**Flag erase.** After the fold (+c = 2^32 + 977 on overflow), k = ctl ∧ [z < y] is erased through a top-32-lane
compare, as before. The compare now uses the same carry-in-free chain (2n + 3 Toffoli). A borrowed carry-in would
break the z = y case, which the Horner product hits at the multiplier's first set bit.

**Fold increments.** The +c fold uses signed-digit increments on borrowed qubits (x −= g; g = ~g; x −= g; g = ~g is
x + 1 for any g). Its subtractions now use the ancilla-free ripple too, so the fold needs no clean carry either.
mod_double and the controlled negation reuse it.

**8-bit size registers.** sy (size of the ring-top pair value) and sx (the spare one, swapped each column) only hold
sizes ≤ NQ = 138, so they are 8 bits. sx is also the first lanes of the estimate's scratch, so the column pool
grows by one lane (68 → 69). One decoder in the map's frame multiply asked the cut register for lane values up to
288 without a range check. A 9-bit register could not match those values, but an 8-bit one aliased them (288 mod
256). That decoder is now range-guarded like the cut walks already were.

## 3. Cost

Average Toffoli 188,053,328 → 185,798,744 (−1.2%). The traversal is unchanged apart from the skipped decoder
steps; the products pay 3n − 2 instead of ~3n per controlled add, and 2n − 2 instead of 2n per fold subtraction.

## 4. Failure budget

The machine and its schedule are unchanged, so the predicted rate is unchanged: model λ ≈ 0.63 expected failing
shots per 9024-shot run. The flag creation is exact, and the flag erase keeps frogdrop's top-32-lane compare
(~2^-32 per add). The nonce predictor found 13 of 24 nonce qubits clean for this op stream. This build keeps
`NONCE = 4`, which is predicted clean and passes all 9024 shots.

**Limiting contract.** The PR 419 limiting contract (copied in full in §6) caps a circuit's λ at 18 on 9,024 shots
and rules out trading error directly for score. This submission does not build on that circuit and stays far under
the cap at λ ≈ 0.63.

## 5. Reproduce

`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit` (or `./benchmark.sh`). The local `eval_circuit` takes ~7 minutes and
~36 GB of memory. `cargo test --release --bin build_circuit` runs the primitive and masked-ladder units, the
modular add and product test (`modp_ctrl_modadd_and_product`), a full traversal against an integer model, the real
203-column schedule on 64 shots, the fold test, and a 64-shot end-to-end point addition (0 mismatches, phase 0,
all ancillas clean). The nonce predictor is the `#[ignore]` test `frogdrop_predict_nonce`

**Result (trusted `eval_circuit` on the empty-environment build, all 9024 shots OK, 0 classical / 0 phase / 0
ancilla):** 937 qubits x 8,138,382 average executed Toffoli = **7,625,663,934**.
Against froghop-single (940 q x 8,738,261, submission 8f53dab): 3 qubits and 599,879 Toffoli fewer (-6.9%), so it
dominates that point on both axes.
**Base:** BitWonka's froghop-single (8f53dab). The traversal (`froghop_single.rs` slot machine, `sched.txt`, W = 314,
900 slots per traversal, 24-deep stack, 96-lane turn discriminator) is unchanged apart from three state qubits (below).
Every truncation point of the modular arithmetic is unchanged. Benchmark files (`src/bin`, `circuit.rs`, `sim.rs`,
`Cargo.*`, `rust-toolchain`) unchanged.

## 1. What changed

### Products: logical-AND carries on the clean qubits below the peak (-597,267 T)

The traversal sets the peak: 937 live qubits (2 x 314 register lanes + 256 passenger + 53 state). The product phases
run with 787 (between the two traversals of a division) or 771 (elsewhere) live qubits including the routines' three
scratch qubits, so 150-166 qubits are clean there. `modp.rs` now hands every clean qubit up to the peak (`PEAK = 937`) to the modular routines as a carry pool:

- **Controlled add** z += a_i * y (256 lanes): the top min(pool, 256) lanes keep their carry on a pool qubit (one
  Toffoli to compute it, uncomputed by an X-basis measurement and a classically controlled CZ); the remaining low lanes
  keep the in-place ripple with the carry in the addend lane. A pool lane costs 2 Toffoli (carry + controlled sum bit)
  instead of 3.
- **Fold** of the overflow (+ c over 65 lanes) and the h (c - 1) correction of the doubling: 64 pool carries,
  64 Toffoli instead of 130. The constant's bits are taken straight from the control qubit, so the 65-lane constant
  register is gone and its qubits join the pool.
- **Overflow-flag erasure** (top-32-lane compare): 32 pool carries uncomputed by measurement, 32 Toffoli instead of 64.
- **Unconditional modadd / modsub:** the carry-out is copied with a CNOT and the uncontrolled ripple is used.

Per Horner step of a product with a 150-qubit pool: 64 (double) + 618 (controlled add: 106 ripple lanes x 3 +
150 pool lanes x 2) + 1 + 64 (fold) + 32 (compare) = 779 Toffoli, was 1,093. Each routine computes exactly the same
function as before (same 65-lane fold truncation, same 32-lane compare), so the failure set of the products is
unchanged.

### Traversal phase: 940 -> 937 qubits (0 Toffoli)

- The sign qubit of the post-traversal sign fix is taken after the traversal state is parked; before, it was taken
  while the whole traversal state was still live, the only 940-qubit moment of the circuit.
- The swap parity lives in the reflection bit: the step-end toggle goes to the reflection qubit, the sign fix needs
  only refl ^ par, and the inverse traversal restores refl before it is used again.
- The RET phase flag is implicit. The phase flags are one-hot, so fr = 1 ^ fo ^ fd ^ fnn: phase transitions drop their
  fr toggles, dn = RET | DIV becomes !(fo ^ fnn), and the two Toffolis controlled by fr (RET with c = 1, and the
  turn-flag erasure) turn fd's qubit into fr with three free gates (fd ^= 1 ^ fo ^ fnn) around them.

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 



The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.



After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.



Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.



Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.



This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.



Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.



The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.



Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.



Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

# froghop-double with ancilla-free offset adds (799 qubits, 17.34M Toffoli: dominates froghop-double 799)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code.
**Result (trusted `eval_circuit` on the empty-environment build, all 9024 shots OK, 0 classical / 0 phase / 0
ancilla):** 799 qubits x 17,340,825 average executed Toffoli = **13,855,319,175**.
Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point. Against froghop-double (799 x 17,366,577): same width, 25,752
Toffoli fewer, so it dominates that point.
**Base:** BitWonka's froghop-double lean build (799 x 17,366,577, submission 37e1f27), unchanged as a machine: registers
D, V (2 x 258) and dy, the 3-bit phase code, rotation counter, stack depth, 6-bit offset boundary, swap parity, the
1240-slot schedule (`sched_double.txt`), every window, the 20-lane discriminator truncation and the point-addition
shell. froghop-double builds on the packed extended-Euclid line of Luo et al. (arXiv:2607.13816). This submission
changes only how a slot uses its scratch; at this width the pool keeps its 7 qubits and the saving comes from the
offset-register adds and counters (section 2). Harness unchanged.

## ELI5

froghop-double's traversal holds the two 258-lane shelves and dy (772 qubits), 20 bookkeeping qubits and a pool of 7
scratch qubits. This build keeps that width and makes the bookkeeping arithmetic a little cheaper: the adds into the
6-bit offset boundary use an adder whose carry chain lives in its own operands (no carry-in or temp qubit), and the
counters drop a constant-1 control. The same build, with the pool shortened, gives the 794-798-qubit points of this
series (section 3).

## 1. Width

| item | froghop-double (799) | this build (799) |
|---|---|---|
| registers D, V (2 x 258) + dy (256) | 772 | 772 |
| phase code, rotation counter, depth, offset boundary, swap parity | 20 | 20 |
| scratch pool | 7 | 7 |
| **total** | **799** | **799** |

The product phases stay at or under 790 (unchanged).

## 2. How

Every replacement below computes exactly the function of the gates it replaces.

- **Offset-register adds** (u +- pi, u +- depth, plain and controlled): the ancilla-free ripple on the low 5 lanes,
  with its carry out XORed into the top lane through one borrowed dy qubit. No clean qubit (was carry-in + temp).
- **Decoders** hold as many prefix levels as the pool allows; the rest of each match is a multi-controlled X on
  borrowed dy qubits (as in the base, now also for the push/pop scan, which held 6 prefixes).
- **Counters:** increments use free pool qubits for carries as far as they go, then borrowed multi-controlled X;
  unconditional increments take bit 0 as the carry control (no constant-1 qubit).
- **Flag predicates as XOR sums of AND terms.** With A = [pi == 0] and B = [depth == 0], a flag such as
  po = CO & !A & !B is CO ^ CO A ^ CO B ^ CO A B; each term is one multi-controlled X on borrowed qubits, so z0 and nz
  are never stored. The same form gives the stack-scan gate, the virtual c_k writes, the CO -> RT marker and the RT0
  logic (RT0 itself is the only qubit those steps hold).
- **u -= po without po:** u -= CO - CO A - CO B + CO A B (inclusion-exclusion; A and B do not involve u), four
  literal-controlled increments of u.
- **Depth decrement at the cofactor ladder's top without po:** depth -= CO !A as depth -= CO, depth += CO A. The CO !A
  shots that had depth 0 wrap to 31. A CO !A shot at depth <= 1 has ct = [depth == 0], so for those shots
  (depth 0, ct = 1) is unreachable and a swap 0 <-> 31 under CO !A ct (CNOT fan-out of bit 0, one controlled flip,
  fan-out again) returns exactly the wrapped shots.
- **Turn scan:** every decoder level is XOR-held in depth bits 0..3 and p1, which are |0> for every turning AL shot
  (garbage elsewhere, restored); the turn gate g joins each lane's 3-control X. The boundary update adds !dl into u
  with one g-controlled increment of the register (!dl, u), which flips !dl back with a CNOT.
- **Masked ladder cells without the cell temp** (only when the pool has no qubit left after the carry-in and the

  with its carry out XORed into the top lane through one borrowed dy qubit. No clean qubit (was carry-in + temp).
- **Decoders** hold as many prefix levels as the pool allows; the rest of each match is a multi-controlled X on
  borrowed dy qubits (as in the base, now also for the push/pop scan, which held 6 prefixes).
- **Counters:** increments use free pool qubits for carries as far as they go, then borrowed multi-controlled X;
  unconditional increments take bit 0 as the carry control (no constant-1 qubit).
- **Flag predicates as XOR sums of AND terms.** With A = [pi == 0] and B = [depth == 0], a flag such as
  po = CO & !A & !B is CO ^ CO A ^ CO B ^ CO A B; each term is one multi-controlled X on borrowed qubits, so z0 and nz
  are never stored. The same form gives the stack-scan gate, the virtual c_k writes, the CO -> RT marker and the RT0
  logic (RT0 itself is the only qubit those steps hold).
- **u -= po without po:** u -= CO - CO A - CO B + CO A B (inclusion-exclusion; A and B do not involve u), four
  literal-controlled increments of u.
- **Depth decrement at the cofactor ladder's top without po:** depth -= CO !A as depth -= CO, depth += CO A. The CO !A
  shots that had depth 0 wrap to 31. A CO !A shot at depth <= 1 has ct = [depth == 0], so for those shots
  (depth 0, ct = 1) is unreachable and a swap 0 <-> 31 under CO !A ct (CNOT fan-out of bit 0, one controlled flip,
  fan-out again) returns exactly the wrapped shots.
- **Turn scan:** every decoder level is XOR-held in depth bits 0..3 and p1, which are |0> for every turning AL shot

  with one g-controlled increment of the register (!dl, u), which flips !dl back with a CNOT.

  running mask): the carry transition f T S and the conditional write g f S are 3-control X gates on borrowed qubits.

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code.
**Result (trusted `eval_circuit` on the empty-environment build, all 9024 shots OK, 0 classical / 0 phase / 0
ancilla):** 935 qubits x 7,519,980 average executed Toffoli = **7,031,181,300**.
Against froghop-single (940 q x 8,738,261, submission 8f53dab): 5 qubits and 1,218,281 Toffoli fewer (-13.9%), so it
dominates that point on both axes.
**Base:** BitWonka's froghop-single (8f53dab). The traversal (`froghop_single.rs` slot machine, `sched.txt`, W = 314,
900 slots per traversal, 24-deep stack, 96-lane turn discriminator) is unchanged apart from the odd-slot step ends and five state qubits
(below).
Every truncation point of the modular arithmetic is unchanged. Benchmark files (`src/bin`, `circuit.rs`, `sim.rs`,
`Cargo.*`, `rust-toolchain`) unchanged.

## 1. What changed

### Products: logical-AND carries on the clean qubits below the peak (-593,677 T)

The traversal sets the peak: 935 live qubits (2 x 314 register lanes + 256 passenger + 51 state). The product phases
run with 787 (between the two traversals of a division) or 771 (elsewhere) live qubits including the routines' three
scratch qubits, so 148-164 qubits are clean there. `modp.rs` now hands every clean qubit up to the peak
(`PEAK = 935`) to the modular routines as a carry pool:

- **Controlled add** z += a_i * y (256 lanes): the top min(pool, 256) lanes keep their carry on a pool qubit (one
  Toffoli to compute it, uncomputed by an X-basis measurement and a classically controlled CZ); the remaining low lanes
  keep the in-place ripple with the carry in the addend lane. A pool lane costs 2 Toffoli (carry + controlled sum bit)
  instead of 3.
- **Fold** of the overflow (+ c over 65 lanes) and the h (c - 1) correction of the doubling: 64 pool carries,
  64 Toffoli instead of 130. The constant's bits are taken straight from the control qubit, so the 65-lane constant
  register is gone and its qubits join the pool.
- **Overflow-flag erasure** (top-32-lane compare): 32 pool carries uncomputed by measurement, 32 Toffoli instead of 64.
- **Unconditional modadd / modsub:** the carry-out is copied with a CNOT and the uncontrolled ripple is used.

Per Horner step of a product with a 148-qubit pool: 64 (double) + 620 (controlled add: 108 ripple lanes x 3 +
148 pool lanes x 2) + 1 + 64 (fold) + 32 (compare) = 781 Toffoli, was 1,093. Each routine computes exactly the same
function as before (same 65-lane fold truncation, same 32-lane compare), so the failure set of the products is
unchanged.

### Traversal: step ends only on odd slots, and 940 -> 935 qubits (-622,000 T)

- **Step ends only on odd slots (-344.6 Toffoli on every even slot).** pi moves by exactly +-1 on every shot in
  every slot (DONE shots oscillate) and is 1 at slot 0, so pi = 0 on a shot means an odd slot. The pi == 0 flag,
  the step end, bit 0 into the cofactor control and the D/V swap (W = 314 Fredkins) are therefore emitted on odd
  slots only; on even slots their gates are identities and RET with c = 1 goes straight to DIV. On 450 of the 900
  slots of each traversal this removes the swap and the pi == 0 logic.
- The sign qubit of the post-traversal sign fix is taken after the traversal state is parked; before, it was taken
  while the whole traversal state was still live, the only 940-qubit moment of the circuit.
- The swap parity lives in the reflection bit: the step-end toggle goes to the reflection qubit, the sign fix needs
  only refl ^ par, and the inverse traversal restores refl before it is used again.
- The RET phase flag is implicit. The phase flags are one-hot, so fr = 1 ^ fo ^ fd ^ fnn: phase transitions drop their
  fr toggles, dn = RET | DIV becomes !(fo ^ fnn), and the two Toffolis controlled by fr (RET with c = 1, and the
  turn-flag erasure) turn fd's qubit into fr with three free gates (fd ^= 1 ^ fo ^ fnn) around them.
- The first-step flag f1 lives in the DONE flag's qubit. f1 is only read in the first 60 slots (the first-step window),
  where no shot can be DONE, so the DONE logic (frozen-slot counter, the DONE oscillation of the rotation, the fnn
  terms of dn and of the implicit RET flag) is simply not emitted there; f1 is 0 on every shot that passes the
  window, and the qubit is the DONE flag from slot 60 on. A shot whose first step outlasts the window failed before
  and fails now. The 60 skipped counter increments save 420 Toffoli.
- One scratch qubit fewer (14 -> 13): the ladder carry-in qubit is idle outside the three ladders, so it also
  carries the termination flag, the first-step erasure flag and the depth counter's top carry, which only live
  between ladders.

| dx, dy and x3, y3 | 3,852 | 1,776 |
| lambda = inv * dy | 279,678 | 199,872 |
| dy phase fix (product + inverse) | 559,356 | 391,552 |
| dx' = lambda^2 - dx - 3 ox (MAC + 3 modsub) | 315,847 | 213,492 |
| ndy = -lambda * dx' | 279,808 | 195,840 |
