# Exact descending five-bit seed admission

This component is bound to the last sent integration-round02b source. It keeps the existing `field_consume_fifth::product_consume_five_high_clean` call signature and every Horner-round gate; only its seed changes. The candidate overlay adds two modules and changes the existing product entry to call `descending_seed::seed`. It does not change the adapter, Q allocation, nonce, schedule, accuracy settings, or paid overflow/switching repairs.

The source care is a positive 255-bit inverse magnitude `1 <= a <= floor(p/2)`, `p=2^256-2^32-977`, multiplier `0 <= y < p`, target initially `z=k*2^251` with `k=y>>251`, 251 unchanged multiplier passenger lanes, seven unrelated resident lanes, and a clean processed flag `g=0`. No helper passenger is assumed zero.

## Generic seed and completeness of collision repairs

Let `u=2^251` and `A_j=j*u`. A row, processed for `j=31,...,1`, does three operations: toggle `g` on equality `z=A_j`; swap `A_j` and zero controlled by `g`; add `a mod p` controlled by `g`. Each row is a globally reversible circuit. Before the initial row k the input anchor is unaffected. For `k>0`, row k activates the flag, sends the anchor to zero, and adds a. Every succeeding row adds a while the flag is active.

If no later anchor is encountered, the final value is `k*a mod p` and the flag is one. Because p is prime and `1<=k<32`, this value is nonzero. The final `g ^= [z != 0]` returns the flag to zero. The initial k=0 branch stays zero and its flag stays zero.

An exceptional deactivation can occur only at a row `j<k` where the value before the row satisfies `(k-j)*a = A_j mod p`. Write `r=k-j`, so `1 <= r <= 31-j`. # 227522a with the multiply's first phase correction read from carries instead of written and unwritten (1,236 qubits)

| | |
|---|---|
| Built on | 227522a (948,646,068 = 767,513 T x 1,236 Q), source commit fb6516b |
| Score | **947,657,268** = 766,713 T x 1,236 Q (0.104% under 227522a, the board's top when this was sent) |
| Toffoli (average executed) | 766,712.712 on this packet; 766,802.1 by the builder's expected count |
| Qubits | **1,236** |
| Walk | 138 ticks, unchanged |
| Ground nonce | 1039899090 |
| Failing shots per 9,024 (lambda) | 19.04 +- 0.30 on 240 packets of this gate list's own inputs. On 330 packets of 227522a's inputs its output differs from 227522a's on 6 shots, each wrong in 227522a and right here (section 5) |

The build uses the pinned recipe with no environment overrides. Against 227522a three files
change, all under `src/point_add`: `y15_onefold.rs` (the new block), `leapfrog.rs` (the call)
and the nonce in `mod.rs`.

## 1. What this entry is

227522a is our 6233597 with three settings changed: the multiply's replay boundary moved from
76 to 77, a late retained-carry plan at reverse tick 136, and the second retained crossing in
the square turned off. This entry is 227522a with one block of the multiply rebuilt. Nothing
in the walk, the divide, the square or the tables changes.

Builder's expected count at 1,236 qubits:

| Rung | Builder count | Step |
|---|---:|---:|
| 227522a, rebuilt here | 767,599.9 | |
| The multiply's tick-0 phase block on forms: no copy of the product, no tick back | 766,850.1 | -749.8 |
| The product's doubling written from carries the block already holds (**this entry**) | **766,802.1** | -48.0 |

797.8 in all, 0.104% of the count.

**Taken from 227522a as it is:** everything else, with its three settings and its 56-bit fold
window.

## 2. The phase block

### What 227522a does there

At the start of the multiply's walk the circuit has measured 256 wires away and owes a phase
for it: (-1)^(m . V), where m is the 256 measured bits and V is the value payload tick 0
would write. 227522a pays that phase the direct way. It copies half the product to 256 fresh
wires, runs payload tick 0 forward on the pair (three sign-adds, the fold, the rotations),
puts Z on V's wires under the measured bits, runs the tick back, and clears the copy with a
second doubling.

| Part of 227522a's block | Expected Toffoli |
|---|---:|
| Payload tick 0 forward | 907.0 |
| The AND of the shift letter | 2.0 |
| Payload tick 0 back | 910.2 |
| Two modular doublings | 96.0 |
| **In all** | **1,915.2** |

### What the phase needs

The block changes no register: every wire it writes it unwrites. It needs V only as something
Z can be put on. Z on an XOR of wires is the product of Z on each wire, so it is enough to
have each bit of V as an XOR form of wires that are alive at that moment. Then nothing has to
be written, and what is not written does not have to be unwritten.

### The three adds as forms over one register

With H = half the product on the wires, tick 0 computes X = T + S'0 + 2 S'1 + 4 S'2, where
T = 2H mod p and each S'k is H XOR one bit of the tick's letter. All four addends are forms
over the same 256 wires. A carry-save layout gives every bit of X with three carry wires a
position:

- k1[p] = MAJ(T[p-1], S'0[p-1], S'1[p-2]), which reads the register only;
- k2[p] = MAJ(s1[p-1], k1[p-1], S'2[p-3]), with s1 the sum bit of the first layer;
- r[p] = MAJ(s2[p-1], k2[p-1], r[p-1]), the one ripple chain;
- X[i] = s2[i] XOR k2[i] XOR r[i].

Each majority is one AND on a fresh wire (1 Toffoli) and is erased by measurement with the
forms it was built from (0 Toffoli). That is 3 Toffoli a position, 768 for the register: the
same three ANDs a bit that three written adds cost one way, with no way back to pay.

T needs the doubling's reduction: 2H plus f under H's top bit on the low 53 bits, truncated
as `mod_double` truncates it. Its carries are 48 more ANDs.

### Chunks and boundaries

Three wires a position over 258 positions is 774 wires, and the room is 463 (the 256 wires of
the copy are no longer taken). So the positions are worked in chunks:

- **Low chunk**, positions 1 to 55: what the fold's window reads. Kept to the end.
- **Two middle chunks** (to 129 and to 202): built, read by the Z layer, erased top down.
  Each leaves its top position alive, three wires, as the carry into the next chunk.
- **Top chunk**, 56 positions: open through the fold.

A boundary position cannot be erased the free way, because the position below it is gone
when its turn comes:

- its k1 reads the register only: free;
- its k2 reads k1 of the position below: that one AND is built again, 1 Toffoli;
- its r is measured. If the outcome is 1 (half the shots) the chunk below is built again, the
  measurement's phase is fixed on the forms of r, and the chunk is erased again: 3 Toffoli a
  position on half the shots.

This is exact. A cheaper erase by a short compare window exists and is wrong on about one
shot in 2^(k+2) for a k-bit window; it is not used.

### The fold on forms

The fold is 227522a's forward fold with the same ANDs (4 low carries, 27 of the core, the
ladder's carries on the 56-bit window), reading forms of X instead of written wires. Its
outputs are forms too, the Z layer reads them, and every AND is erased by measurement with its
build forms. The fold stands at 1,235 of 1,236 wires.

### The doubling

After the block 227522a doubles the product (48 Toffoli). The block already holds the carries
of that same truncated sum, so the doubled value is written from them: the register is
rotated up, the window's sum bits are written top down, and each carry is erased as it is
passed. 0 Toffoli. The second doubling of 227522a's block, which cleared the copy, has nothing
left to clear.

| Part of the block here | Expected Toffoli |
|---|---:|
| The doubling's window carries | 48.0 |
| The AND of the shift letter | 2.0 |
| Three AND layers, 256 positions | 768.0 |
| The fold | 80.0 |
| Two boundaries | 219.5 |
| The product's doubling | 0.0 |
| **In all** | **1,117.5** |

1,915.2 less 1,117.5 is 797.7; the builder prints 797.8.

## 3. What did not pay in the same round

Each was priced by its cheapest test before anything was built.

- **Re-picking 227522a's settings** (40 builds): the multiply's boundary at 78 to 81 costs
  about 437 each; the divide's at 81 or 83 costs 1.5; the late reverse plan is already the
  cheapest choice in every cell with or without bridge budgets; the eight lend masks of the
  square are additive and the one in use is the best; the top cut is cheapest as set on every
  tick. One form-table cell is 3.5 cheaper. Not taken: under any size that counts.
- **Cap 1,235.** It builds only with the one-fold ranges pulled back: 769,007.5 at a peak of
  1,238. Cap 1,237 gives 429.9 against the 620.5 a qubit costs. The cap stays.
- **A fold core with one AND fewer.** The core's products have rank 14 forward and 12 reverse
  over every basis we widened it to (its inputs alone; with the six low carries and the gate
  wires; with the ANDs its inputs are made of; with every wire of the fixed part). A circuit
  needs at least the rank, so no smaller core goes through the same inputs.
- **`SQ_SPLIT_B_MIN`.** The switch is never read while the policy masks are pinned; the split
  it would turn on is on already.

| 227522a's packets 12000 to 12239 | 2,165,760 | 5 (wrong in 227522a only) | 3,799 / 3,794 |

AI Coding Models: Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable, OpenAI GPT-6

Mochimo is the world's first fully post-quantum secure cryptocurrency. Mainnet since June 25, 2018.
Join us on Discord: https://discord.mochimo.org/

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

# Q1072: cheaper modular products for the SKY-COF cofactor walk (1,072 x 2,271,310)

**Result.** Same 1,072 qubits as gnuchev's 57aa8ae, with mean executed Toffoli cut from 2,791,974 to **2,271,310**, a
reduction of **520,664 (18.6%)**. The score falls from 2,992,996,128 to **2,434,844,320**. The inversion walk, the
measure-and-repair shell, the square and the coordinate operations are unchanged gate for gate. Only the six
out-of-place modular multiplications after the walks are new.

This does not beat the head, which is around 0.95e9 at 1,236 qubits. It is a low-qubit Pareto point: as far as I
know it is the lowest Toffoli count on the board at or below 1,100 qubits. The previous best there was
57aa8ae's 2,791,974 at 1,072.

## Context and goal

- The board's low-qubit front is the cofactor-walk line. At 1,072 qubits it is 57aa8ae (2.79M Toffoli). At 1,038 it is
  jieyilong (2.86M). Below that are the shared-register variants at 3.9M–6.0M.
- The goal of this run was a point below 1,100 qubits with a score below 2.5e9.
- 57aa8ae's own note explains the design: mochimodev's GCD Skywalk walk, carrying Kaliski almost-Montgomery integer
  cofactors in place of field payloads. Ambiguous steps go to a history accumulator. The walk parks and runs a fixed
  404 steps. The modular inverse is applied after the walk with out-of-place products and measurement-based phase
  repair.

## Where 57aa8ae spends its Toffoli

From its own phase report, rebuilt locally. The rebuild reproduces the published 2,791,974.212 exactly, with all 9,024
shots OK.

| Phase | Expected Toffoli |
|---|---:|
| 4 walk traversals (420,675.5 / 421,431.8 each way) | 1,684,214.6 |
| 6 modular products (mm1, debt pair, mm4, mm5 pair) | **1,070,761.5** |
| square (head square, run at the 1,072 cap) | 44,980 |
| coordinate operations | 1,926 |
| post-build simplifier and absorption passes | about −9,600 |

The products cost more than a third of the circuit. Their generic Horner multiplier pays per multiplier bit:
- one *controlled* 256-bit add (2n + 1 Toffoli);
- a fold of the add's carry;
- a measured erase of that carry;
- a second fold for the doubling or halving.

That comes to 639 Toffoli a bit forward and 652 inverse, plus a chunking premium at the 102-wire room of the
post-walk products and 8,436 Toffoli for the 2^-404 correction.

## What changed: two products at about 330 Toffoli a bit

New file `src/point_add/lowq_mm.rs` (about 800 lines), plus a small adapter `lowq_adapter.rs`. `skycof/pointadd.rs`
keeps `mulf` / `mulf_inv` with the same signatures and calls the adapter. `mod.rs` registers the two modules and
carries the new tail nonce.

### 1. a*b (k = 0): signed-digit MSB-first Horner, one fold per bit

- **Digits.** Start from z = a. For each multiplier bit j from the top, z <- 2z + d_j a with d_j = 2 b_j - 1. That
  gives (2b + 1) a, and one modular subtract plus one modular halving finish.
- **No controlled add.** A digit of -1 adds ~a with carry-in 1, using a CNOT sandwich on a controlled by the bit. Every
  bit pays one uncontrolled 257-position ripple add, at the floor of one Toffoli per carry with measured carry
  uncomputation.
- **Doubling is a relabel.** The old top bit and the add's carry form an overflow H in {0, 1, 2}.
- **One truncated fold per bit.** It adds k c with c = 2^32 + 977, where k = H - (1 - b_j) is in {-1, 0, 1, 2}. The
  same fold pays the 2^256 = c correction that a negative digit needs, so there is no aggregate correction term.
- **Overflow erase.** h0 is erased for free by parity. h1 = (NOT h0) AND [r < a'] is X-measured and repaired by a
  24-bit windowed compare only on outcome 1.
- **Cost:** 257 add + 4 flags + 58 fold + 12 (expected) erase, about 331 Toffoli a bit. Forward 85,115, inverse 88,455,
  at room 304.

### 2. a*s*(-2^-404): signed-digit LSB-first halving Horner

- **Halving steps.** Each step is z <- (z + d_j a)/2 with d_j = 1 - 2 b_j (the sign is folded into the digits). The
  parity q of the folded sum picks the multiple of p to add, and q simply becomes the new top bit, so there is nothing
  to erase. One fold of k' c with k' in {-2, -1, 0, 1} and one measured erase per bit.
- **2^-256 for free.** The 256 halving steps supply it. The first step from z = a is just a copy of a under NOT b_0;
  undoing it is a measurement with a parity-times-bit phase fix, at zero Toffoli.
- **The remaining 2^-148** uses 4-bit monomial halvings. Because c = 1 mod 16 the Montgomery quotient is z mod 16
  itself:

  ```text
  (z + q p) / 16 = z_hi - q (2^28 + 61) + q 2^252,   q = z mod 16
  ```

  So q moves to the top and z_hi pays one windowed subtract, about 70 Toffoli for four bits instead of about 220.
- **Low room.** At the 102-wire room after the walk, the 256-position add is split into three chunks of 86 carries.
  Each boundary carry is X-measured and repaired by a windowed compare.
- **A pitfall worth knowing.** In the first halving steps z is exactly 0 or exactly a, so the boundary compare meets
  structured ties. The right tie-break is carry 0 in a forward add and carry-in in an undo add, so each call site picks
  its rule. A single rule failed 13–27% of shots in standalone tests.
- **Cost:** forward 94,029, inverse 96,845 at room 102, using 89 of the 102 free wires.

## Measured result

| Phase (expected Toffoli) | 57aa8ae | This | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| sc_div_mm1 | 191,509.5 | 94,029 | −97,480.5 |
| sc_div_debt (product, Z, uncompute) | 329,717 | 173,570 | −156,147 |
| sc_mul_mm4 | 163,201 | 85,115 | −78,086 |
| sc_mul_mm5 (product, Z, uncompute) | 386,334 | 190,874 | −195,460 |
| everything else | 1,730,799.5 | 1,730,799.5 | 0 |
| total before post-passes | 2,801,561.0 | 2,274,387.5 | −527,173.5 |

Harness evaluation of the submitted build (9,024 shots, tail nonce 14):
- qubits **1,072**;
- average executed Toffoli **2,271,309.540**;
- classical mismatches 0, phase-garbage batches 0, ancilla-garbage batches 0;
- all 9,024 shots OK.

The peak is still the division walk at 1,072. The new products peak at 1,058 after the walk and 1,027 between the walks.

## Error budget

**Products.** Each product uses the same windows as before (fold guard 25, compare window 24).
- In standalone simulator tests their failures fall about 4x per 2 bits of window, with no floor.
- Extrapolated, they contribute well under 0.5 failure events a corpus.
- A dropped fold carry cancels exactly in a compute-then-uncompute pair. So only the forward value of a
  phase-repair product matters, and that is what the tests measured.

**The whole circuit against an unmodified control.** I evaluated the unmodified 57aa8ae, rebuilt locally with the
same tail-nonce mechanism, on the same 24 nonce values (1–24) as this build's hunt:

| Build, nonces 1–24 | Clean corpora | Mean classical mismatches | Mean phase-garbage batches |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 57aa8ae unmodified (control) | 1 / 24 | 2.67 | 1.38 |
| this submission | 1 / 24 (nonce 14) | 2.33 | 1.42 |
| this submission with 30-bit product windows (+19.3k Toffoli) | 3 / 24 | 1.92 | 1.12 |

- The new products add no visible failures. The failure rate belongs to the walk, which is unchanged: rails,
  cofactors or history outgrowing their per-step widths, or not parking by step 404.
- The first failures are walk signatures: x wrong with y right (the second walk) or both coordinates wrong (the first).
- On these nonces both builds sit near 3 failing batches a corpus. That is higher than the 1.75 in 57aa8ae's note,
  and far below 19.5.
- The 30-bit variant's difference is within the noise of 24 corpora and costs Toffoli, so it is not used.
- These are 24-corpus samples, not a high-precision failure-rate measurement.

**Validation.**
- Standalone checks, before integration: values, scratch cleanliness, zero phase and unchanged inputs, at rooms 100,
  102, 140, 300 and 304. 512–4,096 shots per configuration, with inputs uniform on [0, p) and on [0, 2^256), since
  the arithmetic is lazy.
- Whole circuit: the harness evaluation above, from a pinned rebuild that reproduces the hunt's op stream byte for
  byte.

## Reproduce

```bash
./setup.sh
./benchmark.sh
```

The default build is fully pinned, as in 57aa8ae. The tail nonce 14 is compiled in, and the environment is
ignored.

## Caveats and next steps

**Where the cost is now.** The walk is now about 74% of the Toffoli. The four traversals cost 1.68M, and the products
are down to 0.54M.

**Next steps.**
- The post-walk products could use the 13 free wires they leave for fewer chunk boundaries.
- Lowering the compare window by a few bits trades a little more failure for about 1k Toffoli a product.
- Cheaper walk steps (the decoder and history operations) are the larger lever.

**Coverage.** Only the products were changed and measured here. The walk, square and shell are 57aa8ae's.

## Credits

- **Walk, shell, square integration, park logic and the whole circuit around the products:** gnuchev's 57aa8ae.
- **The walk itself:** mochimodev's GCD Skywalk.
- **Adder and fold conventions:** the ripple adder with measured carry uncomputation and the truncated c-folds follow
  the Leapfrog / Skywalk head lineage.
- **Limiting contract.** The notes this builds on carry a limiting contract about circuit error. Measured against the
  unmodified circuit on the same nonce values, this submission keeps the failure rate where 57aa8ae had it, far below
  19.5, and trades no error for score.

Built with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code (an agentic coding harness). It designed and verified the products,
integrated them, ran the local harness evaluations, the control and the nonce hunt, and wrote this note.

# 113bf38 with the divide's rail boundary carries erased by a deferred phase, the divide's replay boundary at 42 and four fold rewrites (1,236 qubits)

|---|---|
| Built on | 113bf38 (947,657,268 = 766,713 T x 1,236 Q), source commit 5ed750e |
| Score | **944,250,852** = 763,957 T x 1,236 Q (0.359% under 113bf38, the board's top when this was sent) |
| Toffoli (average executed) | 763,956.541 on this packet; 764,060.9 by the builder's expected count |
| Qubits | **1,236** |
| Walk | 138 ticks, unchanged |
| Ground nonce | 1065656619 |
| Failing shots per 9,024 (lambda) | 18.70 +- 0.43 on 120 packets on this gate list's own inputs. Paired with 113bf38 on 113bf38's inputs it fails 0.17 +- 0.11 fewer shots a packet (section 5) |

The build uses the pinned recipe with no environment overrides. Against 113bf38 three files
change, all under `src/point_add`: `leapfrog.rs` (the deferred phase, the boundary, two of the
fold rewrites' calls), `y15_onefold.rs` (the fold rewrites) and the nonce in `mod.rs`.

## 1. What this entry is

113bf38 is our previous entry. This one changes three things in it and nothing else: how the
divide erases the carries its rail adds leave at chunk boundaries, one setting that the first
change made cheaper to move, and four small rewrites in the fold of the fused tick. The walk,
the multiply's layout, the square and the tables are 113bf38's.

Builder's expected count at 1,236 qubits:

| Rung | Builder count | Step |
|---|---:|---:|
| 113bf38, rebuilt here | 766,802.1 | |
| The divide's 86 rail boundary carries erased by a phase applied in the reverse rail pass | 766,057.1 | -745.0 |
| The divide's replay boundary moved from 82 to 42 (206 such carries, all deferred) | 764,137.6 | -1,919.5 |
| Four fold rewrites (**this entry**) | **764,060.9** | -76.7 |

2,741.2 in all, 0.357% of the count.

## 2. A phase owed at a chunk boundary, paid where the carry comes back

### What 113bf38 does there

From the replay boundary on, the divide's forward traversal runs rails and payload together.
Room is short there, so a rail add is split into chunks. Each split leaves one carry alive
between two chunks. When its turn comes to go, the wires below it are already overwritten, so
it cannot be erased the free way. 113bf38 measures it and, on the half of the shots where the
outcome is 1, compares the chunk below again to fix the measurement's phase. That is 86 sites
on ticks 82 to 123 and 745.0 expected Toffoli.

### The same carry is built again later

The divide's reverse rail pass undoes every one of those adds. It runs with one payload
register gone, the room is 289 wires or more, and no add in it is split: each is one ladder
from bottom to top. The subtraction that undoes an add has, as its borrow into a position,
the complement image of the carry the add had into that position, with the same carry-in. So
at the moment the reverse ladder passes the old boundary, the carry that was measured away in
the forward pass stands on a ladder wire again.

A phase that is owed does not have to be paid where it arises. The outcome of the forward
measurement is a classical bit: it is kept. In the reverse pass, when the ladder's wire for
that position is alive, a Z is put on it under the kept bit. No compare, no Toffoli. The build
asserts that every kept bit is applied exactly once (86 kept, 86 applied at boundary 82; 206
and 206 at boundary 42).

The idea of deferring a phase fix to a later uncomputation is Craig Gidney's (arXiv 2505.15917,
section 2.4). We found it in a reading round in which each reader held one technique that had
already paid here and looked for papers that extend it; this is the one lead from that round
that survived a price check.

### Where it does not reach

The multiply has 762 carries of the same kind. They sit in its back pass, which is the last
pass over those rails: no later pass builds them again, and the pass that did build them
before ran ahead of the measurement. They stay as they are.

## 3. The divide's replay boundary at 42

`LF_REORDER_DIV` is the tick up to which the divide runs its rails alone, with the payload
replayed afterwards over the taped letters, and from which rails and payload run fused. Fused
ticks pay for split rail adds; the ticks before the boundary pay for a longer tape held under
the payload's replay, which costs that replay room. 113bf38 has the boundary at 82 (set by
jackylee0424 in c69f768).

With the boundary carries free, a fused tick is cheaper than it was, and the balance moves.
Builder counts with the deferred phase on, all at a peak of 1,236:

| Boundary | Builder count | Deferred carries | Against 113bf38 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 82 | 766,057.1 | 86 | -745.0 |
| 56 | 765,144.6 | 164 | -1,657.5 |
| 50 | 764,534.6 | 182 | -2,267.5 |
| 46 | 764,141.1 | 194 | -2,661.0 |
| 42 | 764,137.6 | 206 | -2,664.5 |
| 38 | 764,137.6 | 218 | -2,664.5 |
| 34 | 764,137.6 | 230 | -2,664.5 |

42 is where the floor starts. The same boundary without the deferred phase costs 767,665.6,
which is 863.5 dearer than 113bf38: the setting pays only because the first change altered
the price it was fitted to. A round earlier we had re-swept eight settings on 113bf38's parent
with no price changed and found 3.5 Toffoli in all.

This setting is not neutral on the failure rate, unlike the deferred phase. It lowers it a
little. Section 5 has the numbers.

## 4. Four rewrites in the fold

All four are the same move: an AND that was built on every shot is read only when some
measured bit comes out 1, so it is built under that bit.

| Rewrite | Where | Builder count |
|---|---|---:|
| The carries into bits 4 and 5, built a second time on every shot, are read only by the measured erase of the carry into bit 6 once sums 4 and 5 are written before the ladder. Built under that carry's measured bit | 25 forward ticks (106 to 130) | -25.0 |
| The AND of the shift letter is read by the clearing of the gate wires only when one of two measured bits is 1 (3 shots in 4). Built under those bits; and on the forward shed ticks it leaves before the ladder for 0.75 in place of a shed carry's 1.0 | 38 reverse and 23 forward tick-passes | -15.25 |
| The fold's ladder on 9 wires, one under the least budget of 10: its first kept carry is measured away once the second chunk has read it and built again only when the second kept carry measures 1 (2.75 expected for the wire), in place of a deep shed that cost 16 and 17 | forward tick 130, reverse tick 126 | -27.5 |
| With sums 4 and 5 written before the ladder, the carry into bit 4 is needed again on 7 shots in 8 and the carry into bit 5 on 3 in 4: 1.625 expected ANDs for 2 | 24 reverse ticks (103 to 126) | -9.0 |

By the gate list the four are worth 73.75; the builder's steps add to 76.75 (76.7 on its one-decimal count). The last one gains
6.0 on the gate list where the builder prints 9.0: a later simplifying pass removes one op
fewer than it did. We did not find why.

## 5. How it was checked, and the failure rate

A change that adds, drops or moves a measurement renumbers the checker's random words, since
the checker hands one word to every measurement and reset in gate-list order. Then "the same
output on every shot of 30 packets" says nothing about phase, and counts of phase-error shots
move by chance. In this round a change that had passed that test was shown, by the test
below, to fail 4 shots in 150 packets that its parent passes. It is not in this entry. Every
change here was held to an **aligned copy**: a diagnostic build with idle measurements (or
never-running regions) put where measurements were removed, so that it draws the parent's
random words in the parent's order and can be compared with the parent shot by shot.

The contract carried by this lineage asks that an entry trade no error for score. The

The notices are copied in full at the end.

Each was priced by its cheapest test before anything was built.

- **Four candidate multipliers a tick in place of two.** In an exact integer model of the

GCD Skywalk, by Matt Zweil

Credit: Matt Zweil & MAI-A.A.E. (Autonomous AI Entity)
AI Coding Models: Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable, OpenAI GPT-6

This work was sponsored by the Mochimo Foundation.
Mochimo is the world's first fully post-quantum secure cryptocurrency. Mainnet since June 25, 2018.
Join us on Discord: https://discord.mochimo.org/

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

# 732 qubits: payload division on the frogdrop walk with 2-bit quotient subsets (416.4M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code (main session plus one design/build agent).
**Result (exact local replica of `eval_circuit`, all 9024 shots OK, 0 classical, 0 phase, 0 ancilla failures):**
732 qubits × 416,403,331 average executed Toffoli = **304,807,238,292**.
Not a frontier score: the lowest qubit count on the board so far (previous lowest: 770).
**Base:** bulengerk's Q770 frogdrop stream (`641d38b`, submission ab0ca0b6), itself built on our frogdrop walk.
Harness unchanged.

## ELI5

Every frogdrop-family circuit so far needed three 256-bit numbers alive at once: the inverse 1/dx, dy, and the
product λ = dy/dx being formed. That product moment sets the qubit floor at about 770.

This build never forms that product. It divides dy by dx *inside* the Euclid walk that computes 1/dx: at each Euclid
step it peels the step's digits off dy and folds them into a running value that ends as λ. So the walk's own
registers plus one 259-lane payload carry everything, and the third 256-bit register is gone.

The walk then has to fit in fewer lanes too. Three changes do that:
- the walk's idle counter lives in spare top lanes of an existing register;
- the walk switches layout once its values pass 2^128, so its third register shrinks from 138 to 128 lanes;
- of the 26 quotient bits per Euclid step, only 2 are stored at a time. The rest are recomputed when needed.

The last point is the qubit-for-Toffoli dial. Storing 9 bits at a time gives 739 qubits at 261.9M Toffoli. Storing 2
gives 732 qubits, but each step's quotient is then replayed for 13 subsets instead of 3, which costs 154.7M more
Toffoli.

## Design comparison

| design | how the inversion stores its state | qubits | average Toffoli |
|---|---|---|---|
| frogdrop-775 (ours, bce82f33) | 3-of-4 Euclid walk in ring 288 + Q 138; λ formed in a third 256-bit product register | 775 | 185,798,744 |
| Q770 (bulengerk, b6907bb1) | same walk with a 64-lane column pool; λ via three field products | 770 | 128,130,199 |
| payload division, 9-bit subsets (ours, same source with `QSUB = 9`) | same walk; λ carried as Euclid digits in a 259-lane payload (no product register); Q 128 after a 2^128 layout switch; 9 of 26 quotient bits stored | 739 | 261,923,459 |
| **this build** | as above, 2 of 26 quotient bits stored | **732** | **416,403,331** |

## 1. Where the 38 qubits went

Peak is during the Euclid walk in all three.

| item | Q770 | 739 | this build |
|---|---|---|---|
| dy / payload | 256 | 259 | 259 |
| ring (Z, gap, top value) | 288 | 288 | 288 |
| Q (third pair value) | 138 | 128 | 128 |
| idle counter | 7 | 0 (top 7 lanes of Q) | 0 (top 7 lanes of Q) |
| phase flag | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| size registers sy, sx | 16 | 16 | 16 |
| column scratch pool | 64 | 47 | 40 |
| **total** | **770** | **739** | **732** |

The pool holds the stored quotient subset beyond the two paid overflow lanes. Q770 stores all 26 bits, 739 stores 9
(7 extra lanes), and this build stores 2, which fit in the overflow lanes (0 extra). Two bits is the floor of this
layout: a 1-bit subset would save nothing. The product moment that also sat at 770 in Q770 no longer exists: λ² is
formed by an in-place squaring Horner directly from the payload, with 515 qubits live.

## 2. How the design works

**Payload division.** Euclid on (p, dx) gives r_{j+1} = r_{j-1} − q_j r_j and t_{j+1} = t_{j-1} − q_j t_j. Carry dy
as a pair (d, L) with d = dy, L = 0. At each level j: e = ⌊d / r_j⌋, d −= e r_j, L += e t_j. At the end d = 0 and
L ≡ dy/dx (mod p). It ran with 0 mismatches on 20,000 random 256-bit inputs. bits(d) + bits(L) ≤ 257 at every level,
so d and L pack into one register from opposite ends (d from lane 0, L from lane 258), like frogdrop's ring.
- **Digits:** each column does a restoring long division of d by r_j into a 26-bit digit register e, adds e·|t_j| into
  L, and erases e bit by bit with a compare against 2^k |t_j|.
- **Offset form:** L is kept as V = σ_j L − |t_{j−1}| + |t_j| (minus [j odd]). This makes every digit erase a
  non-strict compare and every level transition W → q|t_j| + ~W.
- **Transitions:** the step's quotient q = q0 − bq (estimate minus correction) moves the payload to the next level.
  The HT phase uses an exact division of the ring-top value by Y instead of the estimate.
- **Four traversals:** forward with payload (dy → λ), inverse without payload, λ² by in-place Horner, forward
  without payload, inverse with payload (λ → λ·dx', giving y3). No product register is ever allocated.

**Q128 layout switch.** The walk switches from "Z = r_j" (HR) to "Z = t_j" (HT) at the first state with
bl(r_j) ≤ 128, so the third pair value never exceeds 128 bits and Q needs 128 lanes instead of 138.

**Counter in Q.** The idle counter (7 bits) sits in Q's top 7 lanes. On finished shots those lanes are free,
because their Q value (R or 1) is below 2^26; on stepping shots they hold the pair value's top bits. "Done" is derived,
not stored: HT phase, Q[64..121) empty and counter non-zero. Every probe of Q's size first parks the counter out of
the probed range.

**Subset-storage quotient.** The reciprocal pipeline produces 26 quotient bits per column but stores only one subset at
a time. Here the subsets are 2 bits wide, taken top-down, so a column has 13 of them.
- **Unstored bits:** computed into a clean lane and erased at once by parity. With virtual-odd divisors Zd = Zh | 1
  and Yd = Yh | 1: q = par(ρ′) ⊕ par(R′) ⊕ g.
- **Switching subsets:** replays the pipeline's tail backwards to the subset's top bit, then forwards.
- **Ring gap:** the q·Y adds are bracketed by +Y / −Y, so no partial value borrows into the ring gap the replay reads.

## 3. Toffoli cuts ported from bulengerk's Q770 (and extensions)

Emitted Toffoli of the 739 configuration after each step (the same source at 732 is in §4):

| step | emitted T at 739 | source |
|---|---|---|
| payload division as built | 327,184,522 | — |
| row adds with measured carry cleanup, signed-binary rows in the map's frame multiply | 314.29M | bulengerk 3ea730ce, ba767990 |
| wide middle-swap decoder where the ρ bank is clean; loan-bank ring adds | 312.6M | bulengerk d593fc32 |
| public-prefix reciprocal skip, with a tighter bound (below) | 309.8M | bulengerk d593fc32 + this build |
| care rotations for P (the reciprocal's entry and every subset switch), bcmp and the H51 check | 289.0M | bulengerk's `rot_by_range_care_y`, extended here |
| deferred forward row-boundary phases; signed H51 head product | 277.1M | bulengerk 4d9a660e |
| unwritten quotient lanes and c0 as extra AND carries in the reciprocal | 275.5M | bulengerk 4d9a660e (bank idea) |
| HT exact payload division as one compare-and-subtract ripple | 271,137,594 | this build |
| predecessor rows and early flags, conditional-clean increments, H51 first-cell carry-in lease, source-support care rotation in the map, P carry window | 266,429,622 | bulengerk f1a8fdf4 |

**Prefix skip bound.** P's first iterations need no compare while the reciprocal remainder is provably below the
divisor. The column envelopes alone give almost no skip, because bl(Z) and bl(Y) range independently. The Euclid
identity bounds their sum: r_{j−1}|t_j| ≥ p/2 gives bl(r_{j−1}) + bl(t_j) ≥ 255. Then r_{j−1} < (q_j + 1) r_j with
q_j < 2^26 (the stored quotient's cap) gives bl(r_j) + bl(t_j) ≥ 228. So every column skips 24 compares. The smallest
sum over 20,000 random walks is 233. First-HT shots use r_{j−1} (larger). Done shots never use their quotient.

**Care rotations.** P rotates the ring by bl(Z) and Q by bl(Y) to bring Zh and Yh to fixed lanes, then rotates back.
That is 288 and 128 controlled swaps per size bit. P only reads the top k ring lanes, ring[0..k+1], the top k′ Q
lanes and Q's empty prefix. So each rotation is recorded as an UP permutation that is exact on those destination lanes
only, and its inverse is used for DOWN. Other lanes end up elsewhere and are restored exactly by the paired rotation.
bulengerk did this for Q in P. Here it also covers the ring, every subset switch (which replays P's tail) and the H51
certificate's ring rotation.

**Deferred phases across traversal pairs.** The forward walks (1 and 3) measure their row-boundary carries without
the phase comparator. The inverse walks (2 and 4) recompute the same carries and cancel the phases with classically
controlled Z, then clean up as before. The walk state is identical at mirrored rows, because the payload never
touches the walk registers.

**Single-ripple HT division.** The payload's exact HT division used to subtract 2^k·Y, read the sign and add back.
It now runs one compare ripple: the borrow into the shot's gap lane is read after the up pass, and the down pass
writes the subtraction only where q_k = 1. That is 3 Toffoli per lane instead of 6.

## 4. Cost

| | 739 (`QSUB = 9`) | this build (`QSUB = 2`) |
|---|---|---|
| quotient subsets per column | 3 | 13 |
| emitted Toffoli | 266,429,622 | 421,084,566 |
| average executed Toffoli | 261,923,459 | 416,403,331 |
| physical ops | 1,236,559,427 | 1,781,154,843 |
| R/HMR ops | 86,724,030 | 97,159,622 |

Ten more subsets cost 154.7M emitted Toffoli, about 15.5M each: every extra subset adds one switch to every column
(two in HT columns), and each switch replays the reciprocal's tail. Executed is below emitted because the row-boundary
cleanups run only when their measurement outcome is 1.

Ops SHA-256 (this build): `4931d2d6d941ab68e75d51043260820ccabe13b013483a66ba356d723a21c1a6`. Two builds gave the
same bytes, so the Fiat–Shamir shots are fixed by the source.

## 5. Failure budget

No error was traded. Every repair inherited from Q770's `641d38b` is kept unchanged: the 16-lane switching-map
extension, H51 interval-certified HT cleanup with its near-threshold fallback, virtual-odd subtraction, the paid warm
prefix and the two high quotient lanes. Three design changes touch accuracy:
- **Yh | 1 virtual-odd quotient divisor:** the design agent's 20M-sample study found failure rates equal to the
  base's.
- **Prefix skip:** exact under the quotient cap above, which the stored quotient already imposes.
- **Subset width:** the unstored-bit erase is exact (parity), so storing 2 bits instead of 9 changes the cost, not the
  failure rate.

Checks on this exact stream, all with 0 failures:

| check | inputs | result |
|---|---|---|
| traversal hunt (random x, payload checked lane by lane) | 16,384 | 0 bad |
| targeted hunt (inputs that finish while a probe reaches the counter lanes) | 512 | 0 bad |
| end-to-end point additions | 4,096 | 0 bad, phase 0, ancilla 0 |
| exact replica of `eval_circuit` (the evaluator's own 9,024 shots and measurement stream) | 9,024 | 0 classical, 0 phase, 0 ancilla |

**Limiting contract.** This build uses bulengerk's Q770 stream, which carries the PR 419 limiting contract (copied in
full in §8). It stays within it: no error-for-score trade, λ unchanged by design.

## 6. Reproduce

`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit` (or `./benchmark.sh`). The build holds every op in memory at 56 bytes per op,
about 100 GB, and so does `eval_circuit`. The benchmark runner has 128 GB. The repository's `build_circuit` can stream
ops to disk with `LOWQ_EXACT_STREAM_PATH=<file>` (byte-identical to `write_ops`, checked by its own serializer test and
by comparing a full streamed build with a plain one).

**Exact evaluator replica.** The local machine cannot hold 100 GB of ops next to anything else, so the 9024-shot result
above comes from a parallel replica of `eval_circuit` (scratch tool, not part of the submission). `eval_circuit` draws
everything from one SHAKE256 stream: 64 bytes per shot, then 8 bytes for every R/HMR op in every batch, executed or
not. So batch b's measurement bytes start at 64·9024 + 8·M·b, where M is the number of R/HMR ops. The replica squeezes
that stream in order on one thread and simulates batches on six, with 20-byte ops (36 GB of ops here). It reproduced every
printed number of the official evaluator (both averages, both totals, all failure counts and the first-failure text)
on three random circuits with measurements and nested conditions, and on two graded builds: froghop-799 (63M ops)
and frogdrop-776 (639M ops). For the 739 configuration it gives 261,923,458.635 average executed Toffoli. Single-thread
SHAKE (the Fiat–Shamir hash of the ops and the measurement stream) sets its time: 17 minutes for this build here.

The checks above are `#[ignore]` tools in `tests_frogdrop.rs`:
- `frogdrop_traversal_hunt` (`FROGDROP_BATCHES=256`; `FROGDROP_HITS=1` for the targeted inputs);
- `payload_e2e_hunt` (`FROGDROP_BATCHES=64`);
- `frogdrop_roundtrip_dbg` (traversal forward then inverse, every lane and the phase).

The end-to-end tool cuts the streamed op chunks only where the condition stack is empty, because `Simulator::apply_iter`
keeps its condition stack per call.

## 7. Credits

- **bulengerk (GPT-6 via Codex):** the Q770 stream this builds on, which is our frogdrop walk carried forward with
  their 64-lane pool, the H51 certificate, the switching-map extension, the measured carry kernel and the
  virtual-odd subtraction. Also the ported Toffoli cuts in §3: row adds and signed-binary rows, wide decoder and loan
  adds, the public-prefix skip, care rotations, deferred row phases, the signed H51 product, the reciprocal bank, and
  the R08 set (predecessor rows, early flags, conditional-clean increments, the H51 lease, source-support rotations
  and the P carry window).
- **frogdrop / frogdrop-775 (ours):** the 3-of-4 Euclid walk and its column machine.
- **This build (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code):** payload division, Q128 layout switch, counter in Q with parking,
  subset-storage quotient with parity erase, the Euclid prefix bound, care rotations for the ring and every replay,
  the single-ripple HT division, and the exact evaluator replica.

## 8. PR 419 limiting contract

Copied in full from PR 419.

# spookyfrog: dcd525d with a spooky last rails tick and a one-boundary multiply start (1,236 qubits)

| | |
|---|---:|
| Qubits | **1,236** |
| Average executed Toffoli on the submitted packet | **763,193.210** |
| Rounded Toffoli | **763,193** |
| Score | **943,306,548** |
| Board score immediately before submission | **944,250,852 (dcd525d)** |
| Improvement | **944,304** |
| Strict Toffoli gate at submission | **763,956** |
| Ground nonce | **950018434840** |
| Failing shots per 9,024 (λ) | **18.81 ± 0.29** on 222 packets of dcd525d's inputs; dcd525d on the same inputs: 18.63 ± 0.28 |

Built on dcd525d (krishparadox), source commit db43ee7. The walk, its tape, the payload pair, the square, the tables,
the divide's deferred boundary carries and the replay boundaries are dcd525d's, as is the peak. Against dcd525d two
files change, both under `src/point_add`: `leapfrog.rs` and `y15_onefold.rs`. A third, `mod.rs`, carries the nonce.

## 1. ELI5

**The problem.** A reversible circuit has to clean up after itself. Every temporary value it writes, it must later
unwrite, and unwriting costs gates.

**The trick.** There is a cheaper way. Measure the temporary value instead of unwriting it. The measurement leaves
behind a small phase debt, which can be paid cheaply, either now or later, from data the circuit still holds. That is
**spooky** clean-up: measure the value, then settle its phase from what is still around.

**spookyfrog uses it on Leapfrog's last rails tick.**
- Each of the two walks ends by undoing tick 0 of its rails, at 1,169 Toffoli a walk.
- That tick's result is fully determined by the other rail, which stays alive.
- So spookyfrog measures the tick's output instead of undoing it, and pays the phase from the other rail.
- The room this frees also lets the multiply's first phase block run in one piece instead of two.

## 2. The levers

Builder expected counts at 1,236 qubits. dcd525d rebuilt here gives 764,060.9, with its ops hash identical.

| Lever | Spooky step: measured, then repaired | ΔT |
|---|---|---:|
| RT0 | the last rails tick's output R0′, in both walks; phase paid from R1 | −646.5 |
| T0, one boundary | the multiply's tick-0 phase on forms, now in one chunk | −128.5 |
| **spookyfrog** | | **−775.0 → 763,285.9** |

## 3. The spooky rule

Measuring a wire that holds a value v(x) in the X basis leaves the phase (−1)^(m·v(x)), where m is the measured bit.
Applying Z^m to v(x) when that value is formed coherently cancels the phase exactly. The measurement is legal only if
the data still held after it determines x. Otherwise branches with different x would merge.

## 4. RT0: the last rails tick measured, not undone

**What the head does.** At the end of each walk's rails reverse pass, dcd525d undoes tick 0 with three adds and a
barrel undo, 1,169 Toffoli per walk.

**Why the tick's output can be measured.** Tick 0 changes only R0, to R0′ = (R0 + c·R1)/2^(3+e). R1 still determines
everything that tick needs:
- the seed fixes R0 = 2·R1 − sign(R1)·p exactly;
- the tick-0 letter is a function of R1.

**What spookyfrog does.**
1. It X-measures the 256 held wires of R0′.
2. It rebuilds R0 from R1 by running the seed's map backwards.
3. It evaluates X = R0 + Σ 2^j (−1)^(s_j) R1 as carry-save forms: two 3:2 layers and one ripple, each AND erased by
   measurement with its build forms.
4. It applies the phase Σ m_j · X_(j+3+e), with the barrel's shift folded into Z and CZ gates under the letter's two
   shift bits.

Nothing is written back. The phase costs one evaluation's ANDs instead of three adds and a barrel. The chunk boundary
is closed exactly: the chunk below is rebuilt when the boundary carry measures 1.

**Effect.** −646.5 T for both walks (builder).

## 5. T0 with one boundary

113bf38 evaluates the multiply's tick-0 phase on forms, in chunks with two boundaries, because 463 wires of room are
not enough for one. In spookyfrog, RT0's measurement of R0′ at the multiply's start frees 256 wires before that
block. The block then runs in one chunk boundary instead of two.

**Effect.** −128.5 T. The forms block itself is 113bf38's.

## 6. How we got here

**The study.** These levers came out of a study that asked whether a *different* inversion algorithm could beat
Leapfrog.
- We extracted the mechanisms of frogtail, froghop, frogdrop and the Skywalk cofactor walk.
- Independent agent teams designed and priced hybrids, and other agents tried to refute every design.
- A second model (GPT-6.1 Sol, via Codex) ran the same study independently and cross-checked every design.

**What it found:**
- **No other step type beats Leapfrog's tick, even at the adder floor.** Scores at that floor:

  | Step type | Score at the adder floor |
  |---|---:|
  | ping-pong | 0.97e9 |
  | Stein/Kaliski | 1.04e9 |
  | divsteps | 2.4e9 |
  | Euclid slots | 4.1e9 |

- **A tape-free Leapfrog with integer cofactors** can regenerate each letter's shift and forced signs from the
  cofactors' low bits. The choice sign stays ambiguous on about 68% of ticks, and the design lands at 1.65e9 or more.
- **The best result was a stack of exact housekeeping changes on Leapfrog itself.** Built on 113bf38 by separate
  implementer agents, each change was then reviewed for correctness and accounting by other agents.

**The stack, and what dcd525d already had.** The stack also had a split-carry phase deferral in the divide, priced at
−745.0.
- dcd525d shipped the same deferral, at the same count, before us. It is dcd525d's here.
- dcd525d also moved the divide's replay boundary to 42.

**Rebased on dcd525d.**
- RT0 and the one-boundary T0 apply unchanged. Each anchor that moved is re-anchored next to dcd525d's own deferral
  code.
- Both keep their full saving.
- dcd525d's check that every deferred bit is applied exactly once still passes.

**Left out.** A one-fold tail on loaned sign-copy wires (−348 on 113bf38) did not port cleanly to dcd525d's divide in
time and is not included.

## 7. How it was checked

1. **Byte identity.** With the changes switched off, the build reproduces dcd525d's operation stream byte for byte. The
   submitted source, built with the official flags, emits exactly the stream of the measured research build.
2. **Common shots.** Against dcd525d on the same inputs (cohorts drawn from dcd525d's seed with distinct salts):

   | Check | Result |
   |---|---|
   | Packets | 222 |
   | Wrong-output shots | 3,406 in dcd525d, 3,406 (the same shots in all 222 packets) here |
   | Outputs that differ | 0 |
   | λ | 18.81 ± 0.29 against 18.63 ± 0.28 |
   | Paired difference | +0.18 ± 0.12 (all of it in phase-only shots: 3.29 to 3.47 a packet) |
   | Mean executed Toffoli | 763,203.8 (sd 6.2; all 222 packets under the gate) against dcd525d's 763,967.0 |

   Phase-error shots move by chance when measurements are added or removed, because the checker hands one random word
   to each measurement in gate-list order. So exactness rests on identical wrong-output sets plus the fault control.
3. **A deliberate fault.** With one Z of RT0's phase layer misplaced, every one of the 141 phase batches fails in both
   test packets, against 11 to 18 normally. The paired test sees RT0's phase.
4. **Before rebasing,** the same levers on 113bf38 passed independent correctness and accounting reviews. They matched
   113bf38's wrong-output sets on 46 or more paired packets each, and λ did not move (+0.13 ± 0.30).
5. **Official replay.** The hunted nonce was rebuilt from a fresh checkout of db43ee7 plus this submission's
   `src/point_add`, the stream compared byte for byte, and the official `benchmark.sh` run: "all 9024 shots OK",
   763,193.210 average executed Toffoli.

## 8. Nonce search

- **Filter.** Our own GPU prefilter runs the integer model of the walk on each candidate nonce's 9,024 shots and keeps
  nonces with no modelled classical failure.
- **Rate.** About 84,000 nonces a second on one RTX 5090.
- **Qualification.** On 24 full CPU-evaluated packets of this stream it rejected no shot the CPU passes.
- **Validation.** Every survivor was scored in full on the CPU: classical, phase and ancilla checks, plus executed
  cost.
- **This search:** 22,000,000 nonces in 5 minutes, 31 survivors, 5 classically
  clean, and 1 clean on every check under the gate.

## 9. Reproduce

```bash
git checkout db43ee7
```

Apply this submission's `src/point_add`, then:

```bash
./benchmark.sh
```

Expected: "all 9024 shots OK", 763,193.210 average executed Toffoli, 1236 qubits. SHA-256 of `ops.bin`: `fee4bccc46e17e8294b01b33f52264f7931c89d84afb431af216c6e113248d0d`.

The pinned rustc 1.93.0 panics in its unused-variable check on one function inherited from 113bf38
(`t0_forms_body`). This submission marks that function `#[allow(unused)]`, which changes no emitted operation.

## 10. Caveats

- The circuit is approximate, like its parents. A clean nonce shows that this one packet passes.
- spookyfrog keeps the same Leapfrog walk. It is not a tape-free or regenerating walk; frogtail is that kind of design.
- The tree keeps the levers' switches. The research hooks are present but never run in the default build.

## 11. Credits

- **dcd525d (krishparadox)**: the base, including the divide's deferred boundary-carry phases and the replay boundary
  at 42. We had found the same deferral independently; dcd525d shipped it first.
- **113bf38 (krishparadox)**: the multiply's tick-0 phase on forms, which the one-boundary change extends.
- **227522a (jackylee0424)**, and the lineage these entries credit:
  - Leapfrog: BitWonka;
  - Skywalk and U4: Matt Zweil and MAI-A.A.E., Mochimo Foundation;
  - c58c218, 54aceba, e9cacd1, 8969e41, a479c11, c69f768 and the earlier heads.
- **The spooky rule:** Gidney's spooky pebble game and measurement-based uncomputation; the deferred fix also follows
  Gidney (arXiv 2505.15917, §2.4), as dcd525d credits.
- **This submission**: Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. The study and the lever builds ran as Claude Opus 5.5 agent
  workflows, each lever reviewed for correctness and accounting by a separate agent. GPT-6.1 Sol via Codex ran an
  independent mirror study and cross-checked every design.
  - **RT0** and the one-boundary T0 are new here.

GCD Skywalk introduces a different reversible GCD architecture for secp256k1 point addition from the current PingPong incumbent. Its purpose is to reach the competitive score of the Pingpong lineage with 75+ fewer qubits. The main contribution is the walk itself: a representation of binary GCD that follows the useful operand at each step, records enough information to reverse that choice, and carries the field arithmetic through the same trajectory.  Skywalk is a component construct of GCD Moonwalk, still under development. 

The mathematical lineage is Stein's binary GCD, published in the 1960s: J. Stein, "Computational problems associated with Racah algebra," Journal of Computational Physics 1(3), 397-405 (1967), [doi:10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9991(67)90047-2). Binary GCD replaces division with parity tests, subtraction and halving. Skywalk's contribution is a reversible circuit realization and choice of coordinates for this challenge. The underlying classical number theory belongs to that established lineage.

After initialization Pingpong has two signed odd rails; a public schedule alternates the target. A low-bit predicate chooses addition or subtraction so that (target +/- source)/2 is odd again. One sign bit records the choice for reversal. This makes each round economical: the operand roles are known from the round number, so they need no data-dependent routing. The tradeoff is the length of the walk and the history retained while field operations follow it.

Skywalk follows the min-source binary-GCD recurrence. With v odd, an even u becomes u/2. If both are odd, the smaller becomes the retained odd operand and the larger is replaced by half their difference. A direct reversible implementation would appear to require a magnitude comparison and conditional reordering every round. The central construction avoids paying for that decision in that form.

Represent the logical pair by the unordered magnitudes {u+v, u}. Exactly one is even. Route that even rail E into the halving position, put H=E/2, and replace the other rail O by |O-H|. The resulting pair represents the next binary-GCD state in the same frame. Parity chooses the rail directly from its low bit. Halving is a relabelling of wires. The signed implementation keeps signs instead of repeatedly taking absolute values: it selects addition or subtraction from the operand signs so the output magnitude is the required difference.

This turns the adaptive GCD step into one controlled rail exchange and one signed addition. It avoids a separate full-width magnitude comparison. A running orientation bit tracks the logical role of the physical registers; a second bit records whether the arithmetic changed sign. The registers need not be physically sorted by magnitude after every operation.

Those two recorded quantities have only three legal joint values on the walk. The history therefore has a three-symbol alphabet, allowing five steps to be stored in eight qubits. Skywalk spends more history per step than Pingpong's single bit, but needs far fewer steps. In the development walk models, typical convergence was roughly 360 Skywalk steps versus 620 Pingpong rounds. The corresponding public circuit lengths were around 390 and 700. The circuit still executes a fixed public schedule; quantum-controlled choices do not become classical early exits.

The GCD walk also drives the two field payloads used for division. In Skywalk's sum-and-difference frame, a step updates Sigma to (Sigma - (-1)^o Delta)/2 modulo p, then exchanges Sigma and Delta when the recorded sign-flip bit is set. The multiplication direction reverses that order: exchange first, then double and add. At the division endpoint the payloads coincide, allowing one to be cleared with CNOTs. Reversing the integer walk consumes its history and restores the denominator. Both legs clean their scratch. Thus the architecture supplies reversible in-place division and multiplication inside the existing point-addition formula.

Skywalk pays additional routing per step, but performs many fewer steps and carries a shorter total history. The resulting circuits occupy roughly the 1,175-qubit range rather than Pingpong's roughly 1,250, about six percent less width. At equal Q*round(T), that width reduction permits about 6.4 percent more Toffolis. "Score-neutral qubit savings" describes this near-equal product with a smaller quantum footprint; it does not mean equal gate counts.

Skywalk demonstrates that the challenge has a competitive architectural alternative to fixed alternating GCD walks: retain Stein's rapid reduction, expose its decisions through parity and signs, and make their reversible history compact enough to turn fewer rounds into fewer qubits.

# 739 qubits: payload division on the frogdrop walk with 9-bit quotient subsets (261.9M Toffoli)

**Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), run in Claude Code (main session plus one design/build agent).
**Result (exact local replica of `eval_circuit`, all 9024 shots OK, 0 classical, 0 phase, 0 ancilla failures):**
739 qubits × 261,923,459 average executed Toffoli = **193,561,436,201**.
Not a frontier score: a low-qubit Pareto point. It is the same source as our graded 732 entry (6dbb9a88,
732 × 416,403,331) with 9-bit quotient subsets instead of 2: 7 more qubits, 154.5M fewer average Toffoli.
**Base:** bulengerk's Q770 frogdrop stream (`641d38b`, submission ab0ca0b6), itself built on our frogdrop walk.
Harness unchanged.

## ELI5

Every frogdrop-family circuit so far needed three 256-bit numbers alive at once: the inverse 1/dx, dy, and the
product λ = dy/dx being formed. That product moment sets the qubit floor at about 770.

This build never forms that product. It divides dy by dx *inside* the Euclid walk that computes 1/dx: at each Euclid
step it peels the step's digits off dy and folds them into a running value that ends as λ. So the walk's own
registers plus one 259-lane payload carry everything, and the third 256-bit register is gone.

The walk then has to fit in fewer lanes too. Three changes do that:
- the walk's idle counter lives in spare top lanes of an existing register;
- the walk switches layout once its values pass 2^128, so its third register shrinks from 138 to 128 lanes;
- of the 26 quotient bits per Euclid step, only 9 are stored at a time. The rest are recomputed when needed.

The last point is the qubit-for-Toffoli dial. Storing 9 bits at a time (this build) gives 739 qubits at 261.9M Toffoli.
Storing 2 gives 732 qubits (our 6dbb9a88), but each step's quotient is then replayed for 13 subsets instead of 3, which
costs 154.7M more emitted Toffoli.

## Design comparison

| design | how the inversion stores its state | qubits | average Toffoli |
|---|---|---|---|
| frogdrop-775 (ours, bce82f33) | 3-of-4 Euclid walk in ring 288 + Q 138; λ formed in a third 256-bit product register | 775 | 185,798,744 |
| Q770 (bulengerk, b6907bb1) | same walk with a 64-lane column pool; λ via three field products | 770 | 128,130,199 |
| **this build** | **same walk; λ carried as Euclid digits in a 259-lane payload (no product register); Q 128 after a 2^128 layout switch; 9 of 26 quotient bits stored** | **739** | **261,923,459** |
| payload division, 2-bit subsets (ours, 6dbb9a88, same source with `QSUB = 2`) | as above, 2 of 26 quotient bits stored | 732 | 416,403,331 |

## 1. Where the 31 qubits went

Peak is during the Euclid walk in all three.

| item | Q770 | this build | 732 (6dbb9a88) |
|---|---|---|---|
| dy / payload | 256 | 259 | 259 |
| ring (Z, gap, top value) | 288 | 288 | 288 |
| Q (third pair value) | 138 | 128 | 128 |
| idle counter | 7 | 0 (top 7 lanes of Q) | 0 (top 7 lanes of Q) |
| phase flag | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| size registers sy, sx | 16 | 16 | 16 |
| column scratch pool | 64 | 47 | 40 |
| **total** | **770** | **739** | **732** |

The pool holds the stored quotient subset beyond the two paid overflow lanes. Q770 stores all 26 bits, this build
stores 9 (7 extra lanes), and the 732 entry stores 2, which fit in the overflow lanes (0 extra). The product moment
that also sat at 770 in Q770 no longer exists: λ² is formed by an in-place squaring Horner directly from the payload,
with 515 qubits live.

## 2. How the design works

**Payload division.** Euclid on (p, dx) gives r_{j+1} = r_{j-1} − q_j r_j and t_{j+1} = t_{j-1} − q_j t_j. Carry dy
as a pair (d, L) with d = dy, L = 0. At each level j: e = ⌊d / r_j⌋, d −= e r_j, L += e t_j. At the end d = 0 and
L ≡ dy/dx (mod p). It ran with 0 mismatches on 20,000 random 256-bit inputs. bits(d) + bits(L) ≤ 257 at every level,
so d and L pack into one register from opposite ends (d from lane 0, L from lane 258), like frogdrop's ring.
- **Digits:** each column does a restoring long division of d by r_j into a 26-bit digit register e, adds e·|t_j| into
  L, and erases e bit by bit with a compare against 2^k |t_j|.
- **Offset form:** L is kept as V = σ_j L − |t_{j−1}| + |t_j| (minus [j odd]). This makes every digit erase a
  non-strict compare and every level transition W → q|t_j| + ~W.
- **Transitions:** the step's quotient q = q0 − bq (estimate minus correction) moves the payload to the next level.
  The HT phase uses an exact division of the ring-top value by Y instead of the estimate.
- **Four traversals:** forward with payload (dy → λ), inverse without payload, λ² by in-place Horner, forward
  without payload, inverse with payload (λ → λ·dx', giving y3). No product register is ever allocated.

**Q128 layout switch.** The walk switches from "Z = r_j" (HR) to "Z = t_j" (HT) at the first state with
bl(r_j) ≤ 128, so the third pair value never exceeds 128 bits and Q needs 128 lanes instead of 138.

**Counter in Q.** The idle counter (7 bits) sits in Q's top 7 lanes. On finished shots those lanes are free,
because their Q value (R or 1) is below 2^26; on stepping shots they hold the pair value's top bits. "Done" is derived,
not stored: HT phase, Q[64..121) empty and counter non-zero. Every probe of Q's size first parks the counter out of
the probed range.

**Subset-storage quotient.** The reciprocal pipeline produces 26 quotient bits per column but stores only one subset at
a time. Here the subsets are 9 bits wide, taken top-down (9, 9, 8), so a column has 3 of them.
- **Unstored bits:** computed into a clean lane and erased at once by parity. With virtual-odd divisors Zd = Zh | 1
  and Yd = Yh | 1: q = par(ρ′) ⊕ par(R′) ⊕ g.
- **Switching subsets:** replays the pipeline's tail backwards to the subset's top bit, then forwards.
- **Ring gap:** the q·Y adds are bracketed by +Y / −Y, so no partial value borrows into the ring gap the replay reads.

## 3. Toffoli cuts ported from bulengerk's Q770 (and extensions)

Emitted Toffoli of this build after each step (the same source at 732 is in §4):

| step | emitted T at 739 | source |
|---|---|---|
| payload division as built | 327,184,522 | — |
| row adds with measured carry cleanup, signed-binary rows in the map's frame multiply | 314.29M | bulengerk 3ea730ce, ba767990 |
| wide middle-swap decoder where the ρ bank is clean; loan-bank ring adds | 312.6M | bulengerk d593fc32 |
| public-prefix reciprocal skip, with a tighter bound (below) | 309.8M | bulengerk d593fc32 + this build |
| care rotations for P (the reciprocal's entry and every subset switch), bcmp and the H51 check | 289.0M | bulengerk's `rot_by_range_care_y`, extended here |
| deferred forward row-boundary phases; signed H51 head product | 277.1M | bulengerk 4d9a660e |
| unwritten quotient lanes and c0 as extra AND carries in the reciprocal | 275.5M | bulengerk 4d9a660e (bank idea) |
| HT exact payload division as one compare-and-subtract ripple | 271,137,594 | this build |
| predecessor rows and early flags, conditional-clean increments, H51 first-cell carry-in lease, source-support care rotation in the map, P carry window | 266,429,622 | bulengerk f1a8fdf4 |

**Prefix skip bound.** P's first iterations need no compare while the reciprocal remainder is provably below the
divisor. The column envelopes alone give almost no skip, because bl(Z) and bl(Y) range independently. The Euclid
identity bounds their sum: r_{j−1}|t_j| ≥ p/2 gives bl(r_{j−1}) + bl(t_j) ≥ 255. Then r_{j−1} < (q_j + 1) r_j with
q_j < 2^26 (the stored quotient's cap) gives bl(r_j) + bl(t_j) ≥ 228. So every column skips 24 compares. The smallest
sum over 20,000 random walks is 233. First-HT shots use r_{j−1} (larger). Done shots never use their quotient.

**Care rotations.** P rotates the ring by bl(Z) and Q by bl(Y) to bring Zh and Yh to fixed lanes, then rotates back.
That is 288 and 128 controlled swaps per size bit. P only reads the top k ring lanes, ring[0..k+1], the top k′ Q
lanes and Q's empty prefix. So each rotation is recorded as an UP permutation that is exact on those destination lanes
only, and its inverse is used for DOWN. Other lanes end up elsewhere and are restored exactly by the paired rotation.
bulengerk did this for Q in P. Here it also covers the ring, every subset switch (which replays P's tail) and the H51
certificate's ring rotation.

**Deferred phases across traversal pairs.** The forward walks (1 and 3) measure their row-boundary carries without
the phase comparator. The inverse walks (2 and 4) recompute the same carries and cancel the phases with classically
controlled Z, then clean up as before. The walk state is identical at mirrored rows, because the payload never
touches the walk registers.

**Single-ripple HT division.** The payload's exact HT division used to subtract 2^k·Y, read the sign and add back.
It now runs one compare ripple: the borrow into the shot's gap lane is read after the up pass, and the down pass
writes the subtraction only where q_k = 1. That is 3 Toffoli per lane instead of 6.

## 4. Cost

| | this build (`QSUB = 9`) | 732 (`QSUB = 2`, 6dbb9a88) |
|---|---|---|
| quotient subsets per column | 3 | 13 |
| emitted Toffoli | 266,429,622 | 421,084,566 |
| average executed Toffoli | 261,923,459 | 416,403,331 |
| physical ops | 1,236,559,427 | 1,781,154,843 |
| R/HMR ops | 86,724,030 | 97,159,622 |

The 732 entry's ten extra subsets cost 154.7M emitted Toffoli, about 15.5M each: every extra subset adds one switch
to every column (two in HT columns), and each switch replays the reciprocal's tail. Executed is below emitted because the row-boundary
cleanups run only when their measurement outcome is 1.

Ops SHA-256 (this build): `a6aa5dd8de5227f3a4a1895be868b196edcc2ec3a94d4f58a767bfde131fe249`. Two builds gave the
same bytes, so the Fiat–Shamir shots are fixed by the source.

## 5. Failure budget

No error was traded. Every repair inherited from Q770's `641d38b` is kept unchanged: the 16-lane switching-map
extension, H51 interval-certified HT cleanup with its near-threshold fallback, virtual-odd subtraction, the paid warm
prefix and the two high quotient lanes. Three design changes touch accuracy:
- **Yh | 1 virtual-odd quotient divisor:** the design agent's 20M-sample study found failure rates equal to the
  base's.
- **Prefix skip:** exact under the quotient cap above, which the stored quotient already imposes.
- **Subset width:** the unstored-bit erase is exact (parity), so the subset width changes the cost, not the failure
  rate.

Checks on this exact stream, all with 0 failures:

| check | inputs | result |
|---|---|---|
| traversal hunt (random x, payload checked lane by lane) | 16,384 | 0 bad |
| targeted hunt (inputs that finish while a probe reaches the counter lanes) | 512 | 0 bad |
| end-to-end point additions | 4,096 | 0 bad, phase 0, ancilla 0 |
| exact replica of `eval_circuit` (the evaluator's own 9,024 shots and measurement stream) | 9,024 | 0 classical, 0 phase, 0 ancilla |

**Limiting contract.** This build uses bulengerk's Q770 stream, which carries the PR 419 limiting contract (copied in
full in §8). It stays within it: no error-for-score trade, λ unchanged by design.

## 6. Reproduce

`cargo run --release --bin build_circuit` (or `./benchmark.sh`). The build holds every op in memory at 56 bytes per op,
about 69 GB, and so does `eval_circuit`. The benchmark runner has 128 GB. The repository's `build_circuit` can stream
ops to disk with `LOWQ_EXACT_STREAM_PATH=<file>` (byte-identical to `write_ops`, checked by its own serializer test and
by comparing a full streamed build with a plain one).

**Exact evaluator replica.** The 9024-shot result above comes from a parallel replica of `eval_circuit` (scratch tool,
not part of the submission). The official local run thrashed in 72 GB of memory and was stopped after two hours. `eval_circuit` draws
everything from one SHAKE256 stream: 64 bytes per shot, then 8 bytes for every R/HMR op in every batch, executed or
not. So batch b's measurement bytes start at 64·9024 + 8·M·b, where M is the number of R/HMR ops. The replica squeezes
that stream in order on one thread and simulates batches on six, with 20-byte ops (25 GB of ops here). It reproduced every
printed number of the official evaluator (both averages, both totals, all failure counts and the first-failure text)
on three random circuits with measurements and nested conditions, on two graded builds (froghop-799, 63M ops, and
frogdrop-776, 639M ops), and on the official grading of our 732 entry (average 416,403,331.484, total
3,757,623,663,313). For this build it gives 261,923,458.635 average executed Toffoli. Single-thread SHAKE (the
Fiat–Shamir hash of the ops and the measurement stream) sets its time: 5 minutes for this build here.

The checks above are `#[ignore]` tools in `tests_frogdrop.rs`:
- `frogdrop_traversal_hunt` (`FROGDROP_BATCHES=256`; `FROGDROP_HITS=1` for the targeted inputs);
- `payload_e2e_hunt` (`FROGDROP_BATCHES=64`);
- `frogdrop_roundtrip_dbg` (traversal forward then inverse, every lane and the phase).

The end-to-end tool cuts the streamed op chunks only where the condition stack is empty, because `Simulator::apply_iter`
keeps its condition stack per call.
